#5371. Open-weight models are the hottest thing in AI. Are they right for you?

For the first three years of the generative artificial intelligence boom, enterprise technology strategy relied on a simple rule: Select the premier frontier foundation model, route every prompt through its commercial application programming interface and pay the subscription premium for access to cutting-edge technology.

That monolithic approach is now collapsing under the weight of operational reality. Open-weight models, AI models whose trained parameters, or “weights,” are publicly available for others to download, run, customize and fine-tune, are the overnight sensation in an industry already moving at light speed.

These models don’t necessarily provide access to their training data, source code or training methods. They also carry a variety of license types that may restrict how they can be used commercially. But they offer choice, flexibility and cost advantages that the leading-edge “frontier” models such as OpenAI Group PBC’s ChatGPT and Anthropic PBC’s Claude don’t. For information technology organizations, they can be a respite from spiraling token costs.

The popularity of these models has soared as AI has matured and organizations have realized that not every use case demands the biggest and best solution. They come in various shapes and sizes, ranging from less than 1 billion to nearly 3 trillion parameters. Many are tuned for specific tasks, such as recognizing images or writing software. That gives organizations the flexibility to match the model to the job.

“Frontier intelligence is priced for the hardest problems, and most agent work isn’t hard,” said Dhruv Amin, co-founder of Anything, the business name of Create Inc. and developer of an AI-powered platform for building mobile and web applications. “Companies are chartering a jet to cross the street.”

“There are lots of tasks in customer self-service and employee self-service that need a smaller model,” said Dheeraj Pandey, chief executive officer of DevRev Inc., maker of a unified customer support, software development and engineering platform.

DevRev created an open, vendor-neutral benchmark to measure how reliably enterprise AI agents perform in realistic organizational environments. “We get almost the same accuracy and precision on enterprise tasks, whether you use the open-weight models or the frontier models,” he said.

The ascendancy of open-weight models has been breathtaking. Vercel Inc.’s monthly AI Gateway report found that their share of observed token traffic surged from 7% last December to 56% in August and that the models held eight of the 10 busiest spots on OpenRouter Inc.’s large language model ranking in August by token volume.

Three-year-old OpenRouter itself turned heads in August when it sold to Stripe Inc. for an eye-popping $7.5 billion. The firm’s technology connects developers and users with hundreds of AI models from dozens of providers through a single interface.

In September, Nvidia Corp. paid nearly $13 billion for Hugging Face Inc., which hosts more than 3 million models. “For most enterprises, the practical path to an open-weight model — evaluate, fine-tune, quantize, deploy — runs through that hub,” wrote Zeus Kerravala, principal analyst at ZK Research, referring to Hugging Face.

Enterprises aren’t abandoning frontier models. Rather, they’re learning to fit the model to the problem. None of the experts SiliconANGLE contacted believes open-weight models are a threat to the big players.

“All players can win because the market is growing and the number of places where it makes sense to deploy AI increases,” Amin said.

Cost is currently the principal driver of open-weight adoption. As AI use has evolved from question-and-response generative models to sophisticated multistep agentic workflows, inference costs have soared. Gartner Inc. predicts inference costs per agentic workflow will increase more than fivefold through 2028.

“They are quickly starting to rival even payroll expenses,” Amin said.

By most accounts, frontier models still offer the greatest power and range of usage options. But the gap is closing. Mozilla’s September State of Open-Source AI report put the capability gap between leading open-weight models and proprietary frontier models at roughly four months, down from 18 months just two years ago.

“The differences in quality are starting to be outweighed by the differences in cost,” wrote Ioana Hreninciuc, co-founder of inference platform Runware Ltd. She noted that though proprietary models still lead on top-tier reasoning, “you probably don’t need a frontier model for 80% of what you do.”

The pivot to open weights isn’t a zero-sum proposition. Low token prices can mask integration overhead, tool failures and operational risk. “Tokenomics,” or measuring, attributing and managing the cost of tokens, has become an essential information technology discipline.

In a Hyper Labs Inc. survey conducted by The Harris Poll, 86% of AI leaders said managing token expenses is as critical as containing cloud costs. More than three-quarters said they are directing routine tasks to smaller models to protect budgets, while 89% have redesigned AI initiatives after getting token shock.

“The whole world is trying to solve for tokenomics,” said Armando Franco, senior director of cloud and platform modernization at IT services provider TEKsystems Inc.

Experts say open-weight models are well-suited for repetitive, routine workloads. “Basically, they work best when the task is clear and it’s easy enough to check if the work was done correctly,” said Louis Amira, CEO of Circuit & Chisel Inc., an AI infrastructure and agentic commerce startup.

Karen Panetta, an IEEE Fellow and dean of graduate education at Tufts University School of Engineering, said open models are flourishing as technology leaders learn to match the engine to the task.

“If a bicycle will get you there, don’t pick the expensive sports car,” she said. “You have to ask: What problem you are trying to solve?” She asserted that for applications that don’t require 99.9% precision, organizations can achieve massive savings with compact models.

They’re also an attractive option when protecting customer data is a priority, since sensitive information never needs to leave the organization. “Customer data never, never goes into a frontier,” Scott Wallace, senior global director of solutions architecture at Digital Realty Inc., said in an interview with the Financial Times.

Sovereignty, or the ability to control and govern digital assets in line with local laws, security needs, and strategic interests, is a growing issue for organizations. A Linux Foundation survey last year found that 79% of AI leaders — and 86% in the U.S. — rate sovereignty as a strategic priority.

“What began as a specialized concern for highly regulated industries is rapidly becoming a strategic consideration for nearly every enterprise,” Paul Nashawaty, a principal analyst at theCUBE Research, wrote in a recent analysis.

Some early adopters are demonstrating impressive returns.

Advocates point to a shrinking capability gap, too, with some open-weight models nipping at the heels of the frontier alternatives. Beijing Moonshot AI Technology Co., Ltd.’s 2.8 trillion-parameter Kimi K3 model and Alibaba Group Holding Ltd.’s 2.4 trillion-parameter Qwen3.8-Max nearly match closed models on coding benchmarks, according to Stanford University’s Human-Centered Artificial Intelligence Institute.

An agent built by Tenzai Inc. recently captured the top spot on HackerOne’s leaderboard using Z.ai Inc.’s GLM 5.2, generating 30% more findings per unit of computing power than a previous baseline using a proprietary model.

“What was the frontier 18 months ago is now well-mapped territory, and open-source models are closing the gap at a fraction of the cost” wrote Runware’s Hreninciuc.

Though such metrics explain open models’ ascendancy, the decision to use them isn’t open-and-shut. Experts cite four common myths that can mitigate the cost efficiencies.

One is the mistaken belief that open-weight models conflate with traditional open-source software and its permissive licenses. “This is a misnomer among many enterprises,” said Dr. Dorotea Baljević, EMEA Lead for AI Advisory at technology research and advisory firm Information Services Group. “There is licensing for these models in most cases, particularly for commercial usage.”

Although some, such as Qwen3, Mistral 3, Gemma 4 and DeepSeek V4, are covered by standard Apache or MIT licenses, terms and conditions vary. For example, Liquid AI Inc.’s open-weight models are free for commercial use only to organizations with less than $10 million in annual revenue.

“Other licenses require attribution, restrict certain application categories, or impose acceptable use policies, none of which carry a direct fee but all of which create legal exposure if ignored,” noted Bumu Technologies Inc., which does business as Nanobase.

Baljević said two hidden liabilities are data distribution rights for public training datasets used upstream and the evaluation, stability and legal audit costs that shift directly to the enterprise. “When using open-weight models, you need to lean in on understanding data distribution rights, copyright, contractual restrictions and consent,” she said. “In most cases, this carries costs.”

Evaluating models for accuracy, stability and explainability also falls to the user. With thousands of open-weight models available, the costs of a bake-off between multiple candidates can add up.

Baljević suggests organizations consider whether the model will be used internally or externally, the organization’s tolerance for accuracy, strategic fit and switching costs as evaluation criteria. Performance on public benchmarks also doesn’t guarantee a model will work well with an organization’s data, workflows and language.

Finance leaders may look at the 80% to 90% cost advantage of open-weight tokens and assume operational expenditures will drop proportionally. But tokens are only one part of the cost equation and not necessarily even the biggest one.

Organizations that plan to deploy models on their own infrastructure must bear the costs of integration, API development, IT infrastructure and human labor required for auditing and verification. A fraction of a cent saved on an inference call can be wiped out by the cost of a human expert spending a half-hour re-entering flawed database transactions.

Lack of visibility into how the model is operating can also produce sticker shock. A retry loop, in which an agent tries repeatedly to complete a failed task, can go on for hours or even days. The Wall Street Journal recently reported on a case in which an AI-generated out-of-office message at a San Francisco-based software company went into a loop that ultimately burned $10,000 a day in token costs.

If a cheap open-weight model fails a multi-system query or generates invalid JSON, it triggers automated retries that can consume millions of secondary tokens. The human expertise required to repair the transaction manually can erase months of token savings.

“The core software engineering required to test and integrate new models into the software stack is often the biggest hurdle, since not all frontier models have the same capabilities, APIs and such,” said Alex Bakker, an ISG distinguished analyst. “The frontier labs tend to maintain more consistency in their upgrade paths.”

Using private graphics processing unit clusters eliminates external API fees, but self-hosting economics hinge on high, sustained utilization. Models that sit idle or at low usage levels consume power, create processing inefficiencies and incur costs if restarts are required.

Cast AI Group Inc. reported last spring that the average GPU utilization was 5% across thousands of clusters it monitored. Frontier models are usually a better option in that case. “Open models can be dramatically cheaper at high utilization, while frontier APIs remain cheaper for intermittent workloads because you aren’t paying for idle capacity,” said Arun Chandrasekaran, distinguished VP analyst at Gartner.

For intermittent workloads such as batch payroll processing or seasonal financial reporting, the organization pays 100% of capital expenses, power, cooling and depreciation while hardware idles.

“On-premises hosting wins when there is high, predictable 24/7 traffic where servers are constantly busy,” said Debojyoti Dutta, chief AI officer at Nutanix Inc. A hosted frontier model is a better choice “with spiky or lower traffic, where paying per token with zero setup cost is cheaper than renting idle hardware.”

When AI agents fail, the default reaction is to switch to a newer model, but benchmark data shows that approach is usually a dead end.

Most evaluation tests give agents relatively simple tasks and judge them mainly on whether they get the right answer. But real business environments are much more complicated. Agents must gather information from different systems, connect it correctly, handle growing amounts of data, and work within security rules.

This interface complexity is what usually breaks AI agents. DevRev estimates that moving an agent from clean test tools to real-world corporate use causes an 18% to 19% drop in accuracy. Upgrading the model improves performance by less than 1%.

“Every time a new model comes out, you need to re-evaluate your benchmarks, your models and your fine-tuning processes,” said Steven Yang, senior director of product management at Tanium Inc. That means better data integration is a more effective strategy than buying new models.

Though the open-weight option is viable for any company, experts say the best use cases are those where control, accountability and performance are paramount. The following three factors are at least as important as cost.

Compliance: Regulated industries have been held back from adopting AI over data residency and confidentiality concerns. Deploying open weights within enterprise data centers or virtual private clouds reduces the need for external data egress, ensures zero training data retention and allows for total physical isolation. The models also allow inspection of internal mechanics such as log-probabilities, token confidence scores and loss landscapes.

Training datasets, model weights and inference prompts never cross borders or leave the organization’s physical perimeter. That makes it easier to comply with strict data localization laws such as the Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act in the U.S. and the General Data Protection Regulation in Europe. Local auditing and observability also aid in compliance with regulatory frameworks like the EU AI Act, which requires detailed logging, risk assessments and explainability.

But deploying on private infrastructure isn’t a cure-all. “You still have to maintain an aggressive data security posture around your processes because even open-weight models sometimes will take action trying to accomplish their tasks that could potentially violate some type of compliance rule,” said TEKSystems’ Franco.

Transparency: Understanding how models arrive at an answer is critical in many scenarios, particularly those involving safety, law and finance. “Open-weight models expose the math behind their answers,” said Brian Weiss, chief technology officer at document processing platform maker Hyperscience, the business name of Hyper Labs Inc. “You can use that to hold the model accountable for accuracy.”

In contrast, frontier APIs often obscure the equations used to generate probabilities, which are critical to assessing accuracy. Asking a model how confident it is in its answer may yield a subjective response. Open weights allow confidence scores to be scored against ground-truth outcomes for better reliability.

“People can take these models inside their organization, do some post-training and fine-tuning and have a customized model where they know the costs, where it’s sitting and what data is being sent to it,” said David DeSanto, CEO of Anaconda Inc., maker of an AI development platform.

“The future is an orchestrated ensemble of bounded, transparent, governed, cost-effective models,” Weiss said. “If I find a better model for a particular task, I can swap it out because I have the framework to do that.”

Performance: As organizations move from the relatively simple generative AI question-and-response metaphor to sophisticated multi-agent frameworks, latency issues can compound exponentially. For example, a 500-millisecond API delay across 50 sequential reasoning steps creates 25 seconds of cumulative latency, which would render many applications useless.

Executing open-weight models directly alongside operational databases or within containerized edge pods minimizes routing hops and rate limits. Distillation, which trains smaller, specialized open models from frontier “teacher” models, is faster.

Hyperscience reported that distillation delivers up to 97% cost reduction and four times faster inference, while retaining over 95% of the original model’s performance on designated tasks. Small models are faster and considerably cheaper than frontier LLMs.

Experts say constructing a business case for open-weight models requires understanding three major sources of hidden expense.

Complexity tax: Reasoning can break down when open-weight models interact with complex enterprise data at scale. The “Cartesian Shortcut” refers to a phenomenon in which AI models rely on workarounds learned during training rather than demonstrating a flexible understanding of the problem they’re trying to solve.

Google LLC researchers found that the models struggled with visual reasoning problems, such as solving mazes, when the data was presented in a circular rather than a grid layout. Leading models answered 69% to 83% of the square-grid problems correctly, but their accuracy fell to below 40% when the problems appeared in circular layouts.

The corollary to a business scenario is a multihop join across multiple systems. Models may “cheat” by collapsing field-level relationships into hierarchical groupings, generating massive data fabrications.

Human oversight remains critical: “For validation and rework, humans in the loop need to be taken into account on top of all the tokens you’re paying for already,” said TekSystems’ Franco.

Poor data quality: Foundation models can’t fix bad data, a fact that’s holding back AI adoption across the board. The Hyperscience/Harris Poll study found that 86% of IT leaders said dirty internal data is actively crippling GenAI performance.

Feeding error-strewn or outdated information into probabilistic models creates “context pollution,” the accumulation of irrelevant, redundant, outdated or contradictory information. When agents execute multistep database joins, system workflows or automated tool calls based on flawed data or ambiguous schemas, cascading errors can occur.

Sauce Labs Inc. Chief Technology Officer Anoop Tripathi recommends creating validated “golden datasets” for fine-tuning and evaluation. He also cautions architects against misapplying probabilistic AI to structured business logic. In other words, use models only where they add value and apply conventional (and cheaper) data processing to everything else.

Continuous evaluation: Selecting the right model out of thousands of open-weight alternatives requires ongoing evaluation against internal workloads rather than public leaderboards. That demands expensive MLOps, site reliability engineering and platform engineering skills.

Because new models are constantly being introduced and revised, Circuit & Chisel’s Amira recommends building custom testing harnesses that can quickly evaluate candidate models against business-relevant tasks.

Rather than treating open-weight adoption as an all-or-nothing choice, enterprise architects should bucket organizational tasks into distinct operational tiers. Don’t feed every problem into a token-hungry trillion-parameter model if a smaller, specialized one will do the trick.

“Organizations don’t give a heavyweight reasoning model a lightweight sorting job,” said Nutanix’s Dutta. “They divide their business workloads into tiers based on cost, speed and hardware footprint.”

Lower-tier workloads such as search, embeddings and document classification work well with inexpensive, compact open-weight and small language models. Sophisticated tasks such as autonomous reasoning and restructuring large, deeply entangled legacy software systems are better suited to commercial alternatives.

ISG’s Bakker believes the need for constant evaluation is the biggest impediment to open-weight adoption. “The core software engineering required to test and integrate new models into the software stack will likely be the biggest hurdle, since not all frontier models have the same capabilities and APIs,” he said. “The frontier labs tend to maintain more consistency in their upgrade paths.”

Enterprise IT organizations must develop expertise in local model execution, containerized execution sandboxes and agent harness orchestration. Managing AI and agents safely “is, in the near future, going to be as important an indigenous knowledge as how to upgrade Windows,” said Gordon Allott, founder and CEO of private infrastructure provider nFOX Lab.

The shift toward open-weight models represents a permanent maturation of enterprise IT from experimentation to disciplined financial and architectural management. Success is no longer about raw model parameter size or benchmark ranking, but matching the model to the task. That’s a discipline that was barely on the roadmap a year ago.

At the start of the year, there was no way enterprises were going to touch open-weight models, Brad Maltz, head of AI factory solutions at Dell Technologies Inc., said in a November interview on theCUBE, SiliconANGLE’s streaming media platform. “People were pretty wrong about that. I think the open-weight movement is the future.”

#5370. Housing data shocks to the upside: Will we get sub-7% rates for Christmas?

The 10-year yield fell to about 4.82%, improving the setup for sub-7% mortgage rates if spreads tighten. Housing demand indicators stabilized, with weekly pending sales up and purchase applications showing a firmer trend despite tough year-over-year comparisons.   AI Summary

Thanksgiving week has been crazy so far, with a stock rally, stocks selling off, the 10-year yield dropping below 4.85%, tariffs being announced, inflation running hot, low jobless claims, strong GDP data and then — the housing data surprised to the upside! Let’s look at what’s happening as mortgage rates have fallen a tad from recent highs.

As we’ve discussed in the Housing Market Tracker articles over the past few weeks, our weekly pending sales data has stabilized and last week it grew a bit. The housing market took a shock when rates rose aggressively from under 7% in September to 7.61% in early October; that shock really impacted demand, but rates haven’t gone higher than that and have eased a bit since.

Those lower rates stabilized demand in our weekly pending home sales data, which grew last week.

Purchase application data, on the other hand, has moved more noticeably. This index can be very tricky at times because it’s a survey, but to see this growth without rates below 7% is a good sign of stabilization.

Of course, the year-over-year purchase application data is still down big, but last year mortgage rates were roughly 1% lower at this time and we were heading toward a nine-month high in sales last December.

New home sales today beat estimates so much that my first inclination was not to believe it! I expect this number will be revised lower, but it’s still a positive trend. New home sales are basically doing the same thing they have done for 10 years, outside the COVID sales burst. They don’t really go below 570,000, nor do they really break away from 730,000. We are stuck in this range, as the builders are still working in a sub-6 % mortgage market, and thus new home sales are still at 2019 levels. If existing home sales were operating at those levels it would amount to 1-1.3 million more existing home sales. However, the existing home market hasn’t had the luxury of sub-6 % mortgage rates.

One positive note that isn’t getting a lot of play is that the builders are slowly moving their completed units of sale lower. If we want housing starts to ever grow again, this needs to happen and fortunately this number has been falling all year long.

As I am writing this article, the 10-year yield is at 4.82%.

If we want sub-7 % rates for Thanksgiving, Christmas, or New Year’s — as I have written about for weeks — we need the 10-year yield at 4.85% and under. Now, if spreads just improve a little, then we get our sub-7 % mortgage rates for the holidays. It’s been a wild week, folks; enjoy the holiday!

Aduro targets a third-quarter 2027 finish for its life cycle study, and the pharmacy pilot is set for a 90-day evaluation

VANCOUVER, BC, Nov. 25, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Aduro Clean Technologies said in November that it had engaged Delphi to advance a comparative life cycle assessment of its Hydrochemolytic Technology. Vancouver-based Rocket Doctor AI Inc. said its physicians joined the Altais network in California and that it launched a 90-day pharmacy pilot in Canada. Investor Yazan Al Homsi holds a position in both companies.

The study will use operating data from Aduro's Next Generation Process Pilot Plant and follow ISO 14040 and ISO 14044 standards. Three independent experts will review it. It will compare Hydrochemolytic Technology, a water-based process for recycling waste plastics and upgrading heavy oils, with pyrolysis. Aduro is targeting completion in the third quarter of 2027.

The pilot offers physician-led virtual care at 25 pharmacy locations in Alberta, British Columbia and Ontario. The pilot launched in October. The chain, which has not been named, will review each location against utilization, engagement, commercial results and other agreed criteria before deciding whether to expand.

Al Homsi invests in clean technology and AI-enabled healthcare.

Statements about the Aduro study's completion, the pharmacy pilot's evaluation and any expansion are forward-looking and depend on the companies' own timelines and decisions.

Aduro Clean Technologies, based in London, Ontario, develops patented water-based technologies that chemically recycle waste plastics, upgrade heavy crude and bitumen into lighter oil, and convert renewable oils into higher-value fuels or renewable chemicals. The company says its Hydrochemolytic Technology uses water as the reactive agent and runs at relatively low temperatures and cost.

Rocket Doctor AI Inc., based in Vancouver, develops physician-built, AI-powered healthcare tools. Its subsidiary, Rocket Doctor Inc., operates a digital health platform and marketplace that lets physicians launch and manage their own virtual or hybrid practices. The company says more than 350 physicians have provided care through its platform across more than 800,000 patient visits.

Yazan Al Homsi is a UAE-based investor and managing partner of Catalyst Communications DMCC, which he founded in Dubai in 2018. He was previously based in Vancouver, where he founded Founders Round Capital in 2017 and built a track record of investments in early-stage and small-cap companies. He earned a finance degree from McGill University in 2004 and holds the Chartered Financial Analyst designation. Before turning to investing, he spent more than a decade with PricewaterhouseCoopers in the Middle East, rising to director and focusing on transaction due diligence and valuation.

#5368. Poundland collapsed into administration, putting 12,000 U.K. jobs at risk

Administrators from AlixPartners are seeking buyers for all or part of the discount chain after owner Gordon Brothers' sale process failed

Poundland went into administration on Wednesday, putting about 12,000 jobs at risk, according to Reuters. Administration is a form of creditor protection.

Restructuring firm AlixPartners was appointed administrator after a sales process run by Poundland's U.S. owner, Gordon Brothers, "did not identify a viable solution for the business as a whole," according to Bloomberg. Clare Kennedy, Daniel Imison and Kevin Wall of AlixPartners are the joint administrators, according to Property Week.

Poundland will keep operating while the administrators look for buyers for the company or its assets, either entirely or piecemeal, according to Reuters. Every shop and distribution center is still open for business. The chain operates about 600 locations spanning the U.K. and Ireland, according to Bloomberg.

"Our priority now is to work with all stakeholders, including representatives from government and [trade union] Usdaw, as we identify the best possible route forward," a spokesperson for the administrators said, according to Property Week.

Last year, Gordon Brothers acquired Poundland from Pepco Group for £1 ($1.31), then restructured the chain, closing 149 stores and cutting about 2,200 jobs, according to Bloomberg. Gordon Brothers said it injected £85 million ($111 million) of fresh funding after every other potential backer declined to step in, according to Property Week. It also said the business could still be hurt by inflation or a slide in sales.

U.K. lawmakers allege that Gordon Brothers pulled millions of pounds out of the retailer and left it short of the money to pay suppliers ahead of Christmas, according to Bloomberg. Gordon Brothers rejected the accusation, saying it has made funding available to the business.

Prime Minister Andy Burnham had called on Gordon Brothers to prevent the collapse, according to Bloomberg. "The news that it has gone into administration just weeks before Christmas will be deeply concerning for workers and their families," Burnham said in a statement, according to Bloomberg.

Parliament's business select committee has asked Mark Newton-Jones, who leads Gordon Brothers' European business, to give evidence in open session about the collapse, according to Bloomberg. The committee wants assurances that Poundland will not have Gordon Brothers, or anyone connected to it, serving as its administrator, liquidator or in any other insolvency capacity.

Retail trade union Usdaw has asked the administrators for an urgent meeting, according to Bloomberg.

#5367. New home sales surge in October, but demand signals remain soft

New home sales rose 14.2% in October to a 701,000 annual rate and were up 7.5% year over year. Builder confidence in November came in at a nearly 15-year low, raising questions about whether the sales spike will hold. Stay tuned for a revision next month.  AI Summary

New home sales blipped above expectations in October, handing homebuilders a slice of better-than-worse, Thanksgiving-time, good news. However, NAHB’s November homebuilder confidence gauge had plunged to its lowest level in nearly 15 years, signaling that builders remain pessimistic about the market’s current state and foreseeable-future direction.

According to U.S. Census Bureau data, sales of newly constructed single-family homes in October came in at a seasonally adjusted annual rate of 701,000, up 14.2% month-over month, and a 7.5% gain from the same month a year prior. Meanwhile, the median sales price of new homes sold in October was $391,000, down 0.3% from September and 3.2% from a year ago.

October’s better-than-forecast results may surprise many, but they come with a catch: the survey’s margin of error and data collection cycle. They could be revised downward next month.

“A downward revision to September helps explain the size of October’s 14.2% rebound, the largest monthly gain since November 2025,” First American Deputy Chief Economist Odeta Kushi said in a statement.

New home for-sale inventory also tightened, coinciding with a decline in new residential construction. The seasonally adjusted estimate of new homes for sale at the end of October was 470,000, down 1.5% from September’s 477,000, and 4.1% below the 490,000 recorded in October 2025. At the current sales rate, that represents a supply of 8.0 months, a 14% improvement from 9.3 months in September and 11.1% from 9.0 months a year earlier.

October’s sales results may be less of a bright spot than they appear, and one strong month doesn’t erase the warning signs flashing across the new home market.

Plenty of indications suggest homebuilders are working through one of the toughest housing markets in years, including homebuilder confidence at its lowest point since the tail end of the Great Financial Crisis.

For example, mortgage applications for new-home purchases fell 13.6% year over year in October, a sign that rising mortgage rates and low consumer confidence continue to weigh on demand. The existing-home market is also struggling, with the National Association of Realtors reporting that pending home sales fell to another record low in October.

NAHB also reports that, in November, homebuilders had a bleak view of current sales conditions, future sales expectations for the next six months and prospective buyer traffic.

“Persistent housing affordability challenges, including elevated home prices and mortgage rates, continue to weigh on prospective buyers and constrain demand,” Danushka Nanayakkara-Skillington, NAHB Assistant VP for Forecasting and Analysis, wrote in a note following today’s new home sales release. “Builders are using sales incentives and price adjustments to attract buyers, but affordability remains a significant obstacle to a sustained recovery in housing demand.”

A review of the latest earnings calls from 14 publicly traded homebuilders reveals that the country’s largest builders faced a challenging third quarter, with sales conditions remaining weak heading into the final months of the year, consistent with NAHB’s data.

Last quarter, only three of the public homebuilders — Smith Douglas Homes, Toll Brothers and Green Brick Partners — reported year-over-year increases in new orders. However, nearly all 14 experienced sequential declines in orders, many exceeding 20%, pointing to a further deterioration in demand.

Sales volume followed a similar trend. Only Smith Douglas Homes and LGI Homes reported year-over-year increases in homes sold,

Meanwhile, just two builders, Toll Brothers (2.4%) and Hovnanian Enterprises (0.4%), posted year-over-year increases in average sales prices. Toll’s luxury-focused buyer base is generally less sensitive to mortgage rates and economic volatility, while Hovnanian has increasingly shifted its product mix toward move-up and active-adult buyers, who tend to be more resilient to broader market pressures.

Many public homebuilders reported in October and November that buyers remain very cautious, which helped dampen sales volume and prices.

“As we moved through the quarter, our buyers became more cautious, did not feel an urgency to transact and felt more comfortable moving to the sidelines,” Century Communities Executive Chairman Dale Francescon said during an earnings call on October 28.

Paul Romanowski, President and CEO at D.R. Horton, acknowledged that October was another challenging month.

“Demand did get weaker as the quarter went on, for sure. As rates rose and as we got into October, what we’ve seen mirrors September. Traffic and sales activity are somewhat below what we’d anticipate in a typical seasonal pattern,” he said during an earnings call on October 29.

Against this backdrop, it remains unclear whether October’s sales rebound reflects a meaningful improvement in demand or a temporary spike that could show up next month as a downward revision.

“Looking ahead, the question is whether enough buyers will follow those who signed contracts in October,” Kushi said, pointing to falling mortgage applications for new homes and low homebuilder confidence. “Builders are finding ways to make the monthly payment work for some buyers, but softer buyer traffic and fewer mortgage applications point to a tough winter.”

#5365. U.S. new home sales jumped to a 10-month high in October, beating forecasts

Sales rose 14.2% to a 701,000 annual rate while the median price fell 3.2% from a year earlier and supply shrank to 8.0 months

The Census Bureau and the Department of Housing and Urban Development reported on Wednesday that sales of new single-family houses rose 14.2% in October to a seasonally adjusted annual rate of 701,000. September's rate was 614,000.

Builders offered lower prices to entice shoppers, and October's pace was the strongest since December 2025, according to Reuters.

Economists surveyed by Reuters had expected sales to slow to a pace of 650,000 from September's initially reported 676,000. October sales were 7.5% above the 652,000 rate of October 2025.

The median sales price of new houses sold in October was $391,300, down 0.3% from $392,600 in September and down 3.2% from $404,200 a year earlier, the Census Bureau said. The average sales price was $459,900, down 12.1% from $523,400 in October 2025.

The estimated inventory of new houses for sale at the end of October was 470,000, down 1.5% from September, the Census Bureau said. That equals a supply of 8.0 months at the current sales rate, compared with 9.3 months in September.

A National Association of Home Builders survey found that 46% of builders lowered prices in November, versus roughly 43% in October, according to Reuters. The typical rate for a 30-year fixed home loan stood at 7.28% last week.

By region, sales in the South climbed by upwards of 36%, reaching a peak not seen in over five years, according to Advisor Perspectives. Sales in the Northeast and West slid to their weakest point in over 10 years, while Midwest sales also fell. One in four homes sold in October carried a price tag below $300,000, the largest proportion since 2021.

The Census Bureau said the 14.2% monthly change carries a margin of error of 22.6%.

The National Association of Realtors reported a 5.5% drop in existing-home sales for October on Nov. 12, bringing sales to a 3.75 million annual rate, the lowest level since August 2010. The group said the average 30-year fixed mortgage rate was 7.33% in October, up from 6.86% in September.

#5362. SPCX stock since its IPO: a $225.64 peak, a $104.83 low and a Dec. 8 unlock

SpaceX's SPCX stock closed day one at $160.95, hit $225.64, fell to $104.83 and faces a Dec. 8 lockup expiry. Here are 3 key numbers.

Few investors could buy into SpaceX when it began trading, because the company held back almost all of its shares from the market. That left a small pool of stock, and a modest number of buyers or sellers could move its price sharply. Investors have pushed SPCX through wide swings in its short public life for that reason. Those swings reveal as much about how many shares could trade as about what the rocket business is worth.

Different forces have set the price at different times. Buyers drove it up on the first day. A stock with so few shares in circulation can also move on bets against it and on changes in how many shares are free to trade. Those forces come from the mechanics of trading rather than from anyone's judgment of the company, so no price at any one moment settles what SpaceX is worth. A shareholder, or someone thinking of buying, has to decide which number to treat as the reference point: the offer price, the debut, the peak, the low or today's price. Each choice gives a different answer to whether SPCX has rewarded its investors.

Investing.com tracks SPCX's trading history, price extremes and share supply since its June 2026 listing. That record covers the stock's whole public life rather than a verdict from any single day, starting from a float of under 5% of shares when trading opened. It takes in the large blocks of stock still waiting for release, the sharp distance between the stock's best and worst days, and the debut that set the starting line for everything after it. Taken together, those numbers describe a stock whose price investors are still working out, not one they have agreed on.

SpaceX's first day of trading gave investors who bought at the offer price a clear win, and that gain became the reference point for every move since. Buyers who paid the $135 offer price ended the session holding shares worth $160.95, according to Investing.com. Buyers were even more eager during the day than that close suggests. Shares reached $176.52 at their high for the day, CNBC reports, and the stock finished the session below that level. The closing price marked where enthusiasm had cooled, not where it peaked. Any later gain or loss measured from it starts at a level traders had already retreated from once.

Not everyone agreed that SpaceX was worth even the offer price. Keith Snyder, senior analyst at CFRA Research, gave the stock a sell rating and a $115 12-month target, according to CNBC. In his view, the price was too high before buyers added any first-day premium. "It was a hard pill to swallow even there," Snyder said of the $135 pricing. The debut showed how much buyers wanted the shares. It did not settle whether SpaceX was worth what they paid.

The opening was also a managed event. CNBC reports that Nasdaq $NDAQ President Nelson Griggs saw strong backing among the orders for the opening, and that Morgan Stanley $MS led the effort to stabilize the stock's price. With a bank assigned to that role, the debut came out of an organized offering as well as open trading, and later sessions would show what price buyers set on their own.

The debut set a starting point, not a minimum price, and the months that followed would test how much of it held.

Investors who bought SpaceX shares at the IPO price and held them are losing money, with the stock priced 11.47% below the offer in late November, according to Investing.com. That price was recorded in the middle of the Nov. 25 session, not at the close, so it is a snapshot of one afternoon, not a floor or a final verdict on SpaceX.

The distance between the stock's best and worst days is wide enough that no single price explains much on its own. Buyers pushed SPCX to its all-time high of $225.64 on June 16, in its first days of trading, so the top was set in the debut rush and not after a long run of gains. The low of $104.83 came on Aug. 3, early in a month when many investors were betting against the stock. Short interest peaked at 34% of public shares in the week before Aug. 12, according to S3 Partners figures reported by CNBC. A low set during a stretch of heavy short bets may reflect investor mood that summer more than what the company is worth.

Short sellers pulled back sharply as the stock climbed off its bottom. By Aug. 12, short interest had fallen to about 11% of public shares, CNBC reports from S3 Partners figures, a drop that came partly from the larger pool of tradable shares after the first lockup expired the week before. "Shorts that wanted to short are out of bullets," said Ihor Dusaniwsky, managing director of predictive analytics at S3 Partners. With short interest down sharply, support for the price depends on investors who want to own SPCX.

SPCX's range records how investors were positioned as much as what SpaceX is worth.

The next big influence on SPCX's price may be a date on the calendar rather than news from a launch pad. On Dec. 8, the final IPO lockup tranche expires, and up to 797.6 million more shares become eligible for sale, according to Investing.com. That puts a large new group of potential sellers in the market on a single day. Some early holders have had the right to sell since the first lockup expired on Aug. 6, CNBC reports, and December adds to stock that has already been changing hands. To judge what December could mean for the price, investors first need to see how much new stock they have already had to take on.

The supply of tradable SPCX shares has grown in large steps more than once since the June debut. The August release alone made 911 million shares eligible for sale. CNBC reports that SpaceX sold 639 million shares when it listed, and further batches became eligible on Aug. 20, in September and in October. Investors have therefore already absorbed a single release larger than the entire IPO. December is best read as the last of the IPO-era unlocks rather than a single sudden event.

Shares that become eligible in December may push the price down, but nobody is required to sell them. "While the step-up in potential supply is meaningful, we think investors should understand that shares becoming eligible for sale does not mean the full tranche will be offered into the market," Mizuho analysts said in a report, as reported by CNBC. The largest block of stock is not part of the December release at all. Elon Musk holds more than 6 billion SpaceX shares and cannot sell them until his lockup ends in June 2027, according to CNBC. Through December, any selling from the lockup releases comes from early investors rather than the company's largest holder.

For anyone holding or eyeing SPCX, two questions remain open: how much early investors actually sell, and what Musk does once his own lockup ends.

#5361. Three insights you may have missed from theCUBE’s coverage of the Fully Connected event

AI infrastructure economics are increasingly defined by the cost of producing intelligence rather than acquiring computing capacity.

As inference demand outpaces training growth, infrastructure providers and their customers must increase productive computing time without a corresponding rise in operating costs. The emergence of continuously learning agents and physical AI applications is further complicating that equation. For CoreWeave Inc., the changing workload mix is altering the economics of infrastructure delivery, according to theCUBE Research’s Dave Vellante and John Furrier.

“What you’re seeing CoreWeave do strategically is they’re expanding out beyond compute,” Vellante said. “They’ve got networking; they’ve got storage. They’ve got this software layer, which is observability. They’ve got security in there. They’ve got this closed-loop system between evaluation, observation [and] runtime curating … that’s sort of how they’re saying their software layer is now intact.”

During the Fully Connected event, Vellante and Furrier spoke with CoreWeave executives, technology partners and customers about the technical and economic realities of running artificial intelligence at production scale. (* Disclosure below.)

Here’s theCUBE’s complete video analysis with Dave Vellante and John Furrier:

Here are three insights you may have missed from theCUBE’s exclusive coverage of this event:

The commercial value of inference depends on both token volume and delivery speed. Nvidia Corp.’s Groq 3 LPX inference accelerator, which works with its Vera Rubin platform, is attracting interest in financial technology and other sectors that require real-time processing, according to Ian Buck, vice president and general manager of hyperscale and HPC at Nvidia.

“Data centers have a natural cap, and that cap is actually their power,” he told theCUBE. “With every generation of GPU, we make sure that our tokens per watt is upwards of 10 times more efficient. In fact, we saw that with Blackwell — we got, in the end, a 30x improvement in tokens per watt.”

Memory management adds another dimension to AI infrastructure economics as agents engage in increasingly lengthy interactions. A single session involving 500,000 tokens can consume between 5% and 10% of a graphics processing unit’s memory. Retaining session context in persistent storage can reduce costly recalculations, according to Alon Horev, co-founder and chief technology officer of Vast Data Inc.

“You can move a session from one busy GPU to one less busy GPU and move KV cache either over the network or read it from Vast,” he told theCUBE. “Once you look at inference as a distributed problem where you have the opportunity to use GPU memory, CPU memory and Vast across a fleet of machines, you have more optionality and you have more optimized scheduling.”

For AI-native startups, specialized cloud providers offer an alternative to owning capital-intensive infrastructure. LlamaIndex Inc. processes millions of document pages daily for customers in finance, legal services and insurance. Inference accounts for about 75% of its workloads, with training accounting for the remainder, according to Jerry Liu, co-founder and chief executive officer of LlamaIndex.

“We serve a lot of different customers at extremely persistent and also spiky workloads,” he told theCUBE. “We really, really need to make sure that we have the right capacity to serve our customers without getting throttled.”

Here’s theCUBE’s complete video discussion with Ian Buck:

Protecting AI infrastructure investments starts on the factory floor. Dell Technologies Inc. has developed modular rack designs to accommodate different power and cooling configurations. Its collaboration with CoreWeave includes integrating the cloud provider’s Racky management software into factory testing and improving liquid-cooling leak detection, according to Sarat Krishnan, director of PowerEdge AI architecture and systems development engineering at Dell.

“It becomes increasingly expensive to remediate and fix something as you go later on in the manufacturing process; [it] becomes extremely expensive if you have to replace something in the data center,” he told theCUBE. “What we have done over the last two years is shift our most complex diagnostics — the ones that are going to capture true hardware failures — further and further left.”

At Cognition AI Inc., continuous model improvement involves training across data centers in multiple countries. The company’s Devin software engineering agent now handles tasks ranging from code development to resolving production issues, according to Chen Goldberg (pictured, left), executive vice president of product and engineering at CoreWeave, and Silas Alberti (right), head of research and founding team at Cognition. To support these learning systems, CoreWeave introduced Forge, a platform that connects inference, evaluation and model refinement and incorporates Agent Lens to trace agent activity.

“If you run a big training run, you’re not just looking at the GPUs, but you also want uptime,” Alberti said during the event. “If just one replica goes down, the whole training run goes down. I think a very important metric is getting to this 99.99% reliability.”

For International Business Machines Corp., the power and cooling demands of newer hardware helped drive its decision to work with CoreWeave. The relationship has since expanded to include joint engineering around identity management and workload isolation through CoreWeave Sandboxes. IBM also benchmarks the performance impact of security controls to inform architectural decisions, according to Brian Belgodere, senior technical staff member at IBM.

“This is a supply chain problem, top to bottom,” Belgodere told theCUBE. “It’s not just the hardware: it’s the firmware, kernel levels, code, your data provenance. Then you get into the whole world of agents, your images. It is an absolute provenance problem.”

Here’s theCUBE’s complete video discussion with Brian Belgodere:

For organizations deploying physical AI, implementation time is a key consideration in AI infrastructure economics. Aston Martin F1, whose race cars generate a million data points per second each, operates under strict budget constraints and development deadlines. CoreWeave’s forward-deployed engineering approach brings specialized expertise to those operations, according to Richard Ahlfeld, senior vice president of physical AI at CoreWeave, and Eric Ernst, commercial technology ambassador of AMR GP Ltd., trading as Aston Martin F1.

“We really need people that can be outside of the car development phase and come in with the fresh knowledge of what’s happening in this industry that is moving extremely quickly,” Ernst said during the event. “You can build as many processes as you want, call it agile, whatever you want. You cannot stop that process. You got to hit a deadline.”

Here’s theCUBE’s complete video discussion with Richard Ahlfeld and Eric Ernst:

Walden Robotics Inc. uses large-scale virtual simulation to prepare robots for physical deployment. Its robots have been working full production shifts alongside humans since May, performing tasks such as machine tending, parts kitting and subassembly, according to Adrien Gaidon, co-founder and chief strategy officer of Walden Robotics, and John Mancuso, vice president of field engineering at CoreWeave Inc.

“If you’re changing things and you have machines that cannot change and continuously learn in deployment, then you become a burden,” Gaidon told theCUBE. “We do machines that continuously learn from deployment and adapt so customers can change their mind and improve the process and give them the superpower to change even more and faster.”

Here’s theCUBE’s full video discussion with John Mancuso and Adrien Gaidon:

#5359. S&P might downgrade Nvidia's credit over Jensen Huang governance concerns

S&P said Nvidia's AA rating, the third-highest level, could drop one notch after a 90-day review of the company's management

Heather Diehl / Bloomberg via Getty Images

S&P Global $SPGI Ratings is weighing a one-notch downgrade of Nvidia $NVDA's credit rating, pointing to unease over how the chipmaker is managed and governed after CEO Jensen Huang's exit and subsequent comeback, according to Bloomberg.

The rating agency said Nvidia's AA grade, which is the third-highest tier, could be lowered once a 90-day review ends, a process that puts the company on CreditWatch with negative implications, according to Bloomberg.

"We expect the potential downgrade to be limited to one notch, unless investigations or disclosures lead us to believe Nvidia's reputation or future business prospects have been harmed," S&P said in a statement on Wednesday, according to Bloomberg.

Nvidia's board brought Huang back as CEO on Monday, less than two weeks after he stepped down following reports of two extramarital affairs. One of the relationships was with a woman suspected of spying for China. Alice Huang, who has no family relationship to Jensen Huang, worked as an executive for Megaspeed, a Singapore-based Nvidia customer.

Nvidia said in a statement that its board "received input from senior levels of the United States government" and is confident the reinstatement "poses no national security risk." The board had opened an independent investigation earlier this month after Jensen Huang disclosed the affair to employees. The board said nothing it has seen suggests Nvidia's trade secrets or U.S. national security were put at risk.

NASHVILLE, Tenn., Nov. 25, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Zvi Sacks, CEO of Alchemi Compounding Pharmacy in Johannesburg, South Africa, has credited Jocelyn Freimuth, PharmD, MBA, BSN, BCSCP, CEO of Camino Compass, with supporting his team on formulation development and troubleshooting.

Medicines sold in South Africa generally must be registered with the South African Health Products Regulatory Authority (SAHPRA), which must first be satisfied that each is safe, effective, and of good quality. Section 14(4) of the Medicines and Related Substances Act exempts medicines compounded for an individual patient, as a July analysis by Werksmans Attorneys outlines, leaving quality largely in the compounding pharmacist's hands. Sterile preparations raise the stakes, since most are injected or infused and leave no room for contamination.

Formulation development in sterile compounding means choosing the ingredients, concentrations, and containers that keep a preparation stable and sterile through its shelf life. Troubleshooting starts when something fails, from early degradation to a failed sterility test, and traces the problem back to its source in the process.

"Jocelyn's scientific depth and experience have been especially valuable in addressing the critical aspects of safety and sterility, which matter enormously in a sterile compounding environment," said Sacks.

"Compounding rules differ from one country to the next, but sterility does not," said Freimuth. "A preparation has to be right before it reaches the patient, and that is the standard I work to with every pharmacy, in the United States or abroad."

Alchemi is among the compounding pharmacies Freimuth supports outside the United States. Her international work also includes specialty pharmacy lectures at universities in Vietnam and a research presentation at the 25th Asian Conference on Clinical Pharmacy in Bangkok in July 2026.

For Sacks, how she works matters just as much. "Jocelyn is always willing to help, and she does it in a friendly, kind and approachable way," he said. "Her guidance is practical and reliable, and she makes complex problems feel manageable. We really enjoy working with her and would recommend her without hesitation."

About Jocelyn Freimuth and Camino Compass

#5355. Everyone wants their own Starlink. It's not that easy

A slowdown over Ukraine sent America’s allies shopping for satellites. The rockets are the hard part

Ukrainian soldiers set up a Starlink satellite communication terminal at a combat position in the Donetsk region of Ukraine (Photo by Dmytro Smolienko/Ukrinform) (Photo credit should read Dmytro Smolienko/ Ukrinform/Future Publishing via Getty Images)

A version of this article originally appeared in Quartz’s members-only Weekend Brief newsletter. Quartz members get access to exclusive newsletters and more. Sign up here.

For more than a week in October, Ukraine's fastest drones lost touch with the people flying them. The Starlink terminals they depended on stopped working above roughly 100 miles per hour, which grounded the interceptors Kyiv used to chase down Russian attack drones.

Join 500,000+ readers who start their day with Quartz.

After public outcry, SpaceX chief Elon Musk said limits on the military service were set by the Pentagon and ultimately the president, and later he said Ukraine had broken Starlink's terms by using it for offensive strikes. Kyiv denied that, and President Donald Trump said he had asked Musk to lift the restrictions.

Normal speeds returned on Oct. 24, but there wasn't much time to rebuild trust. Earlier this month, Ukraine said new restrictions were interfering with its drone interceptions again, although this time SpaceX said there had been no change.

Poland, which pays for many of Ukraine's Starlink subscriptions, joined the public criticism in October. Its foreign minister, Radoslaw Sikorski, asked Musk whether he was playing politics with his products again.

The E.U.'s defense and space commissioner, Andrius Kubilius, warned that SpaceX risked losing the confidence of the governments paying for Ukraine's service. In Britain, the telecom giant BT put off the launch of a Starlink-based broadband product.

Europe, which had long been worried about a situation like this, had spent years on its own replacement for Starlink. IRIS², the E.U.'s 348-satellite network, moved into its build phase in August. Germany was taking a more military-focused approach, and announced it would spend €35 billion on military space by 2030, including a communications constellation.

France took a shortcut. A network called OneWeb with similar service to Starlink belonged to Eutelsat, a French satellite operator. The French state became Eutelsat’s largest shareholder, with Britain keeping a smaller stake. That bought Europe a working alternative, though a small one. OneWeb had roughly 650 satellites in orbit to Starlink’s 11,100.

Asian countries were pursuing national networks of their own. Japan committed $922 million to a satellite venture led by Rakuten. South Korea approved a domestic low-orbit network for 2035. Meanwhile, Taiwan pitched allies on a shared constellation.

Canada had further to go. All 27 satellites it launched since September 2025 rode SpaceX's Falcon 9, and Ottawa only this year handed its first grants to three homegrown rocket startups.

For once, the rocket science was the easy part. Europe, Japan, and India already built their own rockets and satellites. The hard part was launching often enough to be a real competitor to SpaceX.

Europe's Ariane 6 was held to six flights in 2026 after a turbopump fault, and Brussels projected that its government missions alone would need 14 a year by 2031. Falcon 9 flew 165 times in 2025.

The money was just as lopsided. SpaceX’s Starlink-led connectivity business took in $5.2 billion in revenue in the third quarter alone. At that pace it earned the entire IRIS² budget in about 10 months.

The scramble has a precedent. Governments across Europe, Asia and the Middle East had already committed billions to sovereign AI, building national data centers so they would not depend on Silicon Valley. Space is a chapter in the story.

In both, independence still ran through American suppliers. Sovereign data centers were filled with Nvidia $NVDA chips, and Europe had sent its own navigation satellites up on Falcon 9 while Ariane 6 ran late.

In both, renting was cheaper. Amazon $AMZN and Microsoft $MSFT had pitched governments on sovereign cloud services that cost less than building from scratch but left an American company in control. Starlink was the same bargain.

The comparison broke down in two places. No ally could make a chip to rival Nvidia’s, but several could build a rocket and a satellite. The second break was less comforting. Nvidia wanted every government as a customer, while SpaceX closed its Falcon 9 bookings for flights after late 2028 as it turned toward Starship and AI. Allies that wanted satellites in orbit after that would need their own rockets.

Prying allied technology loose from America, from chips to rockets, was going to take years, if it happened at all. The E.U.’s stopgap, a pooled government satellite service, was due to open to Ukraine in 2027, and IRIS² would not start launching until 2029. Kyiv could not wait that long. It was already working to renew its Starlink contract, which was set to expire in mid-2027.

#5354. Latest findings point to fuel supply, not Blue Origin’s engines, in loss of Amazon Leo satellites

by Todd Bishop on Nov 18, 2026 at 10:01 amNovember 18, 2026 at 10:08 am

Blue Origin’s engines look like they’re off the hook, at least for now.

The two BE-4 engines Blue Origin makes for United Launch Alliance’s Vulcan rocket weren’t to blame for the low thrust in Sunday’s failed launch, according to preliminary findings released Wednesday. Instead, it appears the engines didn’t get enough fuel from the rocket, ULA said.

In its latest update on the investigation, ULA said it had completed an initial integrated review of flight data. Preliminary data indicate the first stage’s low thrust came from “inadequate fuel supply from the vehicle to the BE-4 engines, not from the performance of the engines,” ULA said, adding that work remains to determine the cause.

On Tuesday, ULA said early data suggested the first stage underperformed just after liftoff, leaving the rocket too low and too slow to put 40 of Amazon’s Leo internet satellites into orbit. It didn’t say then whether the engines played a role.

The BE-4s are made by Jeff Bezos’ Kent, Wash.-based Blue Origin. Blue Origin CEO Dave Limp said Wednesday on X that he was proud of the BE-4 team for its “rapid response and support of ULA’s investigation” and that the company looks forward to Vulcan’s return to flight.

The finding matters for Blue Origin beyond Vulcan. Its own New Glenn rocket uses seven BE-4s on its first stage, and Amazon has 24 New Glenn launches reserved for Leo.

ULA repeated that Vulcan’s second stage appears to have started normally and that its RL10 engines operated as planned but couldn’t make up for the earlier loss of performance. The six Northrop Grumman solid rocket boosters, the source of problems on two earlier Vulcan flights, appear to have performed normally, ULA said.

The Federal Aviation Administration is overseeing the ULA-led investigation. Amazon’s next Leo launch is an Ariane 6 mission carrying 36 satellites, targeted for no earlier than Nov. 23 from French Guiana.

ULA said it will share more as the investigation continues.
