#5352. Inflation in 2026: core PCE never fell below 3% from January to October

CNBC's monthly record shows core PCE inflation at 3.0% or higher from January through October 2026, with headline at 3.8% in October.

Americans kept spending through 2026, and a year of steady shopping can look like a sign that households were doing well. Their savings show something else. Americans set aside 4.5% of their after-tax income in January, according to the BEA, which was a modest margin even before the year's price increases set in. The BEA reports that the share was down to 2.6% in April, which left families that month with far less money put away for a lost job or an unexpected bill. Stubborn inflation can show up in a household budget this way. People keep buying what they need, and a smaller share of what they earn goes into savings.

The strain on household budgets came from prices that stayed high all year, not from one bad month. Core inflation, which leaves out food and energy, tracks that underlying pressure. Even in February, one of the months when core inflation ran at its lowest of the year, core prices were up 3.0% from a year earlier, according to the BEA. The best months still left everyday goods and services costing noticeably more than they had the year before. Food and energy prices rose sharply in some months and eased in others, and those changes moved the overall inflation rate up and down. The underlying rate moved within a much narrower range and never fell far. Inflation in 2026 did not rise steadily, and it never cooled enough to give households relief. It stayed high.

CNBC tracked how U.S. consumer price inflation changed across each month of 2026. Over those months, underlying inflation cooled during the summer, and prices rose again in the autumn as energy and transport costs climbed. The October figures are the most recent. The Federal Reserve aims for inflation of 2.0%, and underlying inflation did not come close to that goal in any of those months. Read one month at a time, the year looks less like a steady climb than a series of ups and downs that never brought prices near the Fed's target. The question for the months ahead is whether the autumn rise is a new problem or the same one returning.

The inflation problem that defined 2026 was already in place when the year began, before any spring jump in food or energy prices. In January, core prices, which leave out food and energy, were up 3.1% from a year earlier, according to CNBC. The BEA reports that the full basket of consumer prices, food and fuel included, was up a smaller 2.8%. The pressure came from the everyday goods and services that make up most of a household budget rather than from the grocery aisle or the gas pump. Cheaper gas or groceries could not bring the rate down, because they were not what was pushing it up. Whatever happened to food and energy later in the year happened on top of a base that was already too high.

Households had more real income in January, but they bought only a little more with it. The BEA reports that real disposable income, meaning income after taxes and inflation, rose 0.7% in the month, while consumer spending grew just 0.1% once price increases are taken out. For that one month, income outpaced prices, and households had more real money to spend even as their carts held little more than before. Higher income helped families keep up, but it did nothing to lower the prices underneath it. The core rate that set the year's starting point remained in place.

January looked calm only because a month of strong income covered a problem that was already built into prices.

February's inflation came from the everyday core of household budgets, not from the gas pump or the grocery store. The full price index climbed 0.4% over January, according to Bureau of Economic Analysis data reported by CNBC, and the BEA reports the same monthly gain for the core measure, which sets food and energy aside. Leaving out the most volatile items removes none of the month's increase. Food and fuel prices tend to jump and then settle back, but pressure that runs through the rest of the household budget does not fade on its own.

Households paid for that broad rise by spending more money on barely more goods. Consumer spending rose 0.5% in dollars in February, according to the BEA, but it grew just 0.1% once higher prices are taken out. Almost all of the extra money went to cover price increases, and people came home with close to what they had bought in January. Their buying power shrank at the same time. Disposable income after taxes and inflation fell 0.5% for the month, so households kept up their spending on a smaller real income. Steady spending on falling real income leaves a gap that families have to cover somewhere.

February's rise ran through the whole budget, with no single shock for families to wait out.

In March, the part of inflation that leaves out food and energy stayed high and showed no sign of easing. Core prices were 3.2% higher than a year earlier, according to CNBC, and the BEA reports that they rose 0.3% from February alone. March brought a sudden jump in overall prices, but the more lasting problem was that the base underneath that jump kept going up every month. Whatever happened to groceries and fuel that spring, households already faced an underlying rate above 3%.

The jump that made March stand out came from food and energy, not from a broad new wave of price increases. Overall prices were 0.7% higher than in February, according to the BEA, far faster than the core measure. Core leaves out only food and energy, so those two categories account for the difference. That was the spring pattern of a stuck year, with sharp increases in the cost of essentials on top of a base that kept rising at a steadier pace. A narrow increase was still no comfort to a household, because it hit the purchases people can't put off.

When groceries and fuel cost more, the same paycheck buys less right away. Households ended March with less buying power than they had at the start of the month, as real disposable personal income, which is income after taxes and adjusted for prices, fell 0.1%, according to the BEA. That drop is small on its own. But it came while the underlying rate stayed above 3%, and that combination is how a stuck year costs families: not through a single shock, but through a steady loss of buying power that one bad month makes larger.

March's jump came from essentials, but the base beneath it kept climbing.

The spring's jumps in food and fuel prices had become, by April, the level households were living with rather than one-off shocks. Core inflation, which leaves out food and energy, ran 3.3% above a year earlier, according to CNBC. BEA reports the same rate in its first estimate of the month, so there is little doubt about where the underlying base stood. In that same estimate, the full price index was up 3.8%. Core leaves out only food and energy, so the gap means households paid extra for groceries and fuel on top of a base that would not come down. They faced pressure from two directions at once: a stubborn base, and a costlier layer of essentials above it.

Prices that high left households with less buying power, and the loss held up when the figures were revisited. Real disposable income, meaning take-home pay after taxes and inflation, fell 0.5% in April, BEA reports, and BEA shows the same drop in its May release. At first glance, that looks like a budget under strain from both sides, with prices rising while income went nowhere. Total personal income did not grow at all in April, but the weakness came from falling income for farm owners rather than from paychecks across the workforce. The income dip is more likely a one-off than a sign that jobs or wages were weakening. The lasting problem was prices.

With the income dip set aside, April left a level of price pressure that set the bar for the rest of the year.

Households in May faced a broader rise in prices than the underlying rate alone would suggest. Core prices, which leave out food and energy, were 3.4% higher than a year earlier, according to CNBC, while the BEA reports that the full basket of consumer prices was up 4.1%. The underlying rate did not break loose in May. Core leaves out only food and energy, so the higher overall figure means those two categories had become more expensive than the rest of the budget over the previous 12 months. For a family, the higher number is the one that counts, because groceries and gas are purchases no one can skip.

Shoppers spent more freely in May, but much of the extra money only covered higher prices. The BEA reports that consumer spending rose 0.7% in dollars during the month and only 0.3% once price changes are taken out. The busy checkout lines of May reflected inflation as much as demand. Households paid noticeably more and came home with only modestly more.

Incomes kept pace with spending in May, though part of the gain came from federal aid to farmers. Personal income rose 0.7% in dollars, matching the rise in spending, according to the BEA, and farm income in the month was tied to payments under the American Relief Act of 2025. May's income figure combines ordinary earnings with government aid to a single industry. Only the earnings show how most households were doing as prices kept rising.

In May, households paid more for essentials while the core rate kept creeping up.

June brought a monthly drop in prices but little relief for households. Prices slipped 0.1% from May, according to the first estimate from the BEA. Over 12 months, though, prices were still up 3.5%, according to CNBC. One cheaper month did little to undo a year of increases. For a family, June's bills stayed well above those of the previous summer, even though they stopped rising for a moment.

The first count made June look hotter than the later figures do. In its first estimate of the month, released July 30, 2026, the BEA puts the annual rate at 3.7%, a figure it later replaced. Neither reading comes close to the pace policymakers want. The open question is how much prices eased over the summer, not whether inflation was beaten.

The June drop most likely came from food and energy rather than from underlying prices. The BEA reports that in the same first estimate, core prices, which leave out food and energy, still rose 0.1% while the headline index fell. Underlying inflation did not pause in June. Cheaper groceries and fuel offset it for a single month, and the stubborn base underneath kept rising.

The relief households got in June depended on the most volatile prices they pay, and those prices can rise again as quickly as they fell.

Whether underlying inflation cooled in July depends on which count of the month a reader trusts. By the later count, core prices, which leave out food and energy, were 3.0% higher than a year earlier, according to CNBC, down from 3.3% in June. In its first estimate for the month, BEA puts the annual core rate at 3.3%, the same as June's. By that first count, underlying inflation held still from June to July rather than easing. One count shows a real summer dip, and the other shows no change at all.

The gap between the two counts does not have to mean that one of them is wrong. The 3.3% reading was the first estimate for July, and BEA reports that an annual update of its figures was still to come after that release. The 3.0% reading comes from a record of the full year compiled months later, so revisions may account for the cooler number. Nothing in the figures shows that they do. That leaves the summer cooling an open question. Anyone who reads 2026 as the year inflation eased in summer is relying on the more favorable of the two counts.

Under either count, July gave households a pause rather than relief. Americans bought almost nothing more than they had in June. Spending adjusted for prices rose by only $1.3 billion in July, according to BEA, which is close to no growth at all in an economy the size of the U.S. Households did not buy more even in a month when the underlying rate, by the later count, had cooled. A cooler number on paper and flat buying in stores add up to a pause, not a recovery.

Whatever July's true reading, the problem had not ended when autumn arrived.

By late summer, households got a break from rising underlying prices, but the break only returned them to where the year began. Core prices, which leave out food and energy, were 3.0% higher in August than a year earlier, according to CNBC. That cooled rate held until inflation picked up again in the fall. Core inflation had already sat at that same low in winter, so households ended the summer no better off on underlying prices than they had been in February. A lull that puts prices back at the starting line is a pause, not progress.

The overall cost of living stayed higher than the core reading suggests. With food and fuel included, everything households bought cost 3.4% more than a year earlier, still above the cooled underlying rate. Prices also went on rising during the quiet month, up 0.3% from July, and BEA reports the same monthly increase in its own count. Even in the calmest stretch of 2026, households paid more.

What set August apart was that households bought more with the money they spent. Spending adjusted for prices rose 0.5% in the month, according to BEA, which outpaced the month's rise in prices. Americans came home with more goods and services rather than just bigger bills. That is what a real lull looks like for a family, which gets more for its money instead of only paying more for the same things.

August was the last month of 2026 so far in which households got more for their money.

Prices picked up again in September. The overall price index climbed 0.5% from August, according to Bureau of Economic Analysis data reported by CNBC. Much of the increase came from energy and transport costs, which Americans pay to fuel their cars and get around. Households can't easily cut back on those costs.

The underlying rate of inflation rose more slowly than the headline rate. Core prices, which leave out food and energy, were up 0.3% in September. The core measure leaves out only food and energy, so those two categories account for the gap between the core and overall readings. The underlying rate still moved in the wrong direction, and its annual pace edged up from its late-summer low. Volatile food and energy costs added to a base that was rising again. The autumn increase looks more like the year's old problem returning than a new one starting.

Shoppers paid the full rise in prices at the checkout, not the slower core rate. Once price increases are taken out, consumer spending grew by less than 0.1% in September, according to the BEA. Nearly all of the extra money households spent went to higher prices, and they brought home about the same goods and services as the month before. Their income fell at the same time, with disposable income after taxes and inflation down 0.3% for the month.

Americans kept spending more dollars while their real income shrank, which left them less room to absorb the next price increase.

Inflation was still running hot in October, the most recent month with data. Everything households bought cost 3.8% more than a year earlier, according to Bureau of Economic Analysis figures reported by CNBC. That pace is far from what the Federal Reserve aims for. Setting aside food and energy offers little comfort, because core prices were up 3.3% over the same 12 months, and the underlying rate had climbed back up after its cooler stretch in the summer. With the full measure above the core, food and energy added pressure on top of an already high base rather than causing the problem on their own.

October itself brought no pause. Overall prices rose 0.3% within the month, and core prices climbed at the same pace even with food and energy left out. For households, the squeeze did not ease as the year drew toward its close, and the goods and services they buy became more expensive again.

November's figures come out on Dec. 23, 2026, and will show whether prices finally ease or hold at this level into the new year. Until then, October's numbers show an underlying rate that rose again in the autumn, and as long as it stays high, household paychecks will buy less.

October's data showed both overall and core prices still rising.

#5351. Tech Moves: Microsoft names 2 leaders, loses 1; DoorDash VP departs; BluePill, Glacis get execs

Tech Moves covers notable hires, promotions and personnel changes in the Pacific NW tech community. Submissions: [email protected]

by Lisa Stiffler on Nov 18, 2026 at 12:47 pmNovember 19, 2026 at 11:47 am

— Weiwei Yang has left Microsoft after more than a decade to co-found a startup that is “building the power grid for the AI age,” according to her LinkedIn profile.

Yang was most recently a senior director with Microsoft Research, working on grid technology. Her team built a grid dataset and released small foundation models to help users operate and expand electrical infrastructure.

Yang thanked her community at the tech giant, adding, “I hope the relationships and collaborations we’ve built continue well beyond Microsoft, and that we find many new ways to work together.”

— Allie Mellen has joined Microsoft as principal director for security research and threat intelligence. Mellen was previously a principal analyst at Forrester. She also wrote “Code War,” a book that explores cyberattacks as a powerful geopolitical weapon.

In her new role, Mellen said she will lead strategy for protection and threat intelligence, “helping shape what intelligence we produce, how AI can improve its speed and quality, and how we turn that knowledge into better protection for customers.”

— Agility Robotics, the Salem, Ore., company that had its Nasdaq debut earlier this month, has announced three leadership changes:

— Former tech executive Drew Sheriff has been named CEO and president of the Space Needle and Chihuly Garden and Glass. Sheriff was previously a vice president at DoorDash and has held leadership roles at Amazon, Starbucks and Parachute Home. His roles focused on customer experience, product growth, strategy and marketing.

“His skill set is the ideal background for charting how we attract customers and how we delight customers in this new age,” Jeff Seely, board chair for the Space Needle and Chihuly Garden and Glass, told the Seattle Times.

— Microsoft has named Caroline King as director of its Washington state community and philanthropy team, with a focus on advocacy work across housing, affordability and other priority issues.

King is the founder and past CEO of Washington STEM, an organization that coordinates research, advocacy, policy, philanthropy and partnerships to support science, technology, engineering and math education in the state. She most recently served as a leader on the governing body of an international school in Luxembourg.

— Longtime Amazon and Microsoft tech exec Scott Wiltamuth has retired — mostly.

Wiltamuth joined Amazon in 2011 as an AWS vice president overseeing a large organization building developer and management tools. In 2018, he took a seven-month leave for colon cancer treatment. After returning, he sought a director-level position and thanked company leaders for helping him find a better fit. “Their flexibility and creativity enabled me to extend my AWS career,” he said.

Wiltamuth launched his tech career at Microsoft in 1993 and left nearly 19 years later as director of program management for Visual Studio Pro.

He now spends time with his wife and family, traveling, golfing, swimming and reading. “I don’t plan to pursue another full-time operational role,” Wiltamuth said, “but may do some part-time work.”

— Adam Nygate has exited Palo Alto Networks to co-found and lead a stealth startup based in Seattle. He was founder and CEO of Huntr, a platform launched in 2019 where security researchers could submit information on AI and machine learning vulnerabilities. Protect AI acquired Huntr, and Palo Alto Networks later acquired Protect AI.

“Huntr was a bet that open source gets safer when vulnerabilities are visible to the people who can fix them, even when that made life uncomfortable for vendors who’d rather keep things quiet,” Nygate said in a post announcing his career change and impending new baby.

— BluePill, a Seattle-based marketing startup that helps brands predict consumer behavior, has named Mike Weis as chief revenue officer and head of sales.

Weis has 40 years of experience in consumer packaged goods, retail and commerce, beginning his career as a Pacific Northwest leader at Unilever and holding executive positions at Catalina and Quotient Technologies. Recent roles include adviser at Contento2, eGateway Capital and And1 Advisors.

“Beyond the incredible résumé, Mike is one of the kindest, most genuine, and most passionate people I’ve met. Someone who has accomplished so much, yet brings so much humility, curiosity, and energy to every conversation,” said Ankit Dhawan, CEO and founder of BluePill.

— Glacis, a Seattle startup that builds tamper-proof records of AI behavior, has named Caer Mistral Sanders as a technical co-founder. Sanders has launched startups and joins Glacis from Thoughtworks. Before that, she held leadership roles at Wayfair and Onshape. As a teenager, she published a book on mixed-reality control systems and won a world robotics championship.

In a post announcing the new role, Sanders said she has designed medical record systems, researched robot communication, patented cryptographic technology and built widely used AI platforms. “This is the first time in my career I get to bring all of those skills to bear on one problem, and I couldn’t be more excited!” she added.

— The PNW Battery Collaborative has welcomed Jason Demeny as its director of communications. Demeny is a marketing leader whose past employers include Crusoe, Patch, Qualtrics and Apptio. Earlier in his career, he spent more than a decade at Microsoft over two stints, most recently leading teams that served the Azure Partner Experience group.

The nonprofit PNW Battery Collaborative brings together startups, innovators and researchers focused on energy storage.

— Tom Wheeler, former chairman of the Federal Communications Commission, has joined the advisory council for Known, a Bellevue, Wash.-based company building accountability infrastructure for autonomous AI. Wheeler led the FCC from 2013 to 2017.

Known, previously called Identity Digital Innovation Labs, spun out of Identity Digital in September.

— Versium has promoted Matthew Baumgartner to vice president of engineering. The Redmond, Wash.-based company provides data and software that help businesses identify potential customers, fill in missing contact information and target their marketing. Baumgartner has been with Versium since 2018.

— Charlie Trillingham has been named communications manager for the University of Washington AI and Machine Learning for Engineering programs and the UW NSF AI Institute for Dynamic Systems. He previously served as a marketing and communications lead for the Buerk Center for Entrepreneurship within the UW’s Foster School of Business.

Editor’s note: Story updated 11/19 to correct that Charlie Trillingham worked for the Buerk Center for Entrepreneurship within the UW’s Foster School of Business, not the Foster School itself.

#5349. AI infrastructure stocks continue their slide, but Anthropic closes higher

Investors continued to offload artificial intelligence infrastructure stocks today, but Anthropic PBC recouped some of its losses from earlier this week.

The AI selloff reportedly began in August. It accelerated on Nov. 17, the day Nvidia Corp. CEO Jensen Huang resigned over his affair with a former executive of Megaspeed, a cloud provider under investigation over alleged export control violations. Huang returned to the helm of the chipmaker this past Monday.

Nvidia closed at $173.73 the day before Huang’s resignation. It dropped as low as $125 during the executive’s two-week hiatus and surged 30% on Monday, the day he returned. Nvidia lost some of its recent gains in today’s trading session: its share price closed 3.8% lower.

Other AI chip stocks have also taken a hit. Broadcom Inc. closed a small fraction of a percent lower than yesterday, while Advanced Micro Devices Inc. and Intel Corp. fell 1.56% and 0.57%, respectively.

The semiconductor stock that logged the biggest drop today is Ambarella Inc., a relatively low-profile maker of AI image analysis chips. Its accelerators are used by edge devices to process footage from their cameras. Ambarella dropped 19.77% today after closing 19% lower yesterday.

The stock’s decline was driven not so much by the broader AI selloff, but rather the weak earnings that Ambarella posted on Tuesday. The company missed expectations across the board. Ambarella said that some customers had canceled or delayed orders to mitigate the financial impact of soaring memory prices.

Micron Inc., one of the world’s top memory chip suppliers, saw its market capitalization drop more than 4.5% today. That’s despite CEO Sanjay Mehrotra’s recent disclosure that the company has already sold out 75% of its 2027 manufacturing capacity. According to the executive, the gap between memory demand and supply is only set to increase next year.

Companies downstream from chipmakers in the AI data center supply chain fared better. Hewlett Packard Enterprise Co. ended the trading session 1.75% higher after dipping into the red earlier today, while Dell Technologies Inc. gained 0.64%.

In contrast, the major cloud providers weren’t left out of today’s selloff. Amazon.com Inc., the cloud market’s largest player, closed 3.12% lower. Microsoft Corp. and Google LLC dropped 1.25% and 2.02%, respectively. Oracle Corp., which trails the three companies in market share but has emerged as an important AI infrastructure provider, took the biggest hit: it’s down 5.09% from yesterday.

Anthropic ended the trading session with a 1.08% gain. The company thereby recouped some of yesterday’s losses, which pushed its stock below its $80 debut price. Anthropic went public last week through a record-setting offering that raised more than $93 billion.

Overall, the tech-heavy Nasdaq gained 0.61% while the S&P 500 slid 0.25%. The Dow Jones Industrial Average climbed 0.33%.

#5348. ‘Sister isn’t free’: Melinda French Gates fact-checks viral ‘SNL’ sketch on eldercare

Geek Life: Fun stories, memes, humor and other random items at the intersection of tech, science, business and culture.  SEE MORE

by Kurt Schlosser on Nov 18, 2026 at 1:23 pmNovember 18, 2026 at 1:23 pm

A “Saturday Night Live” skit about caring for aging relatives touched a viral nerve after it aired over the weekend, including with Melinda French Gates, who offered her own “fact check” on the too-close-to-home comedy.

The sketch, a fake commercial, stars host John Mulaney as a man who has found an easy way to care for his aging father without upending his own life: “Sister,” an “elder care system” that is free and is, in fact, his sister.

French Gates wrote on Instagram this week that the sketch “is funny because it’s a little too true.” Using research from Pivotal, her investment and philanthropic organization, she went through the ad’s claims one by one and found that most held up:

Sister will provide. True, French Gates said, citing AARP and the National Alliance for Caregiving. Among adults ages 55 to 64, women are nearly 40% more likely than men to care for an older relative, and nearly 40% more likely to provide constant care.

She’ll quit her job. “Mostly true,” at least the job part. Catalyst found that 42% of women who voluntarily left jobs in 2025 cited caregiving as the main reason.

Paid help is pricey. “True, unfortunately.” New America puts the average home health aide at more than $6,600 a month, and 24-hour care can top $25,000.

Sister may break down. Also true. In the Caregiving in the U.S. 2025 report, nearly two-thirds of caregivers said they were under moderate or high emotional stress, and women felt the strain more than men did.

“Free” is misleading. French Gates said Sister isn’t free; she’s the one paying for the care, in lost wages, stalled careers, thinner retirement savings and less time for her own life.

French Gates has made women’s health and caregiving central to her work since she stepped down as co-chair of the Gates Foundation in 2024.

She left with $12.5 billion to put toward her work on behalf of women and families. Much of that work runs through Pivotal, the Seattle-area organization she founded to handle her philanthropy and investments. In June she pledged another $215 million for women’s health, which brought her giving in that area to more than $600 million over two years. The pledge included $10 million to the Menopause Society for better menopause care in the U.S.

The sketch has been shared widely across the country this week, in part because it lines up so closely with the research.

In its own analysis, The New York Times cited studies showing that daughters generally provide at least twice as much care to aging parents as sons do. The U.S., unlike many wealthy countries, offers no federal paid leave or long-term care insurance for family caregivers.

French Gates said she welcomed the conversation.

“I’m so glad we’re talking about this, and laughing about it,” she wrote on Instagram. “We need more honesty about what caring for loved ones really takes and why so much of that work falls to women. But I’d love for the day to come when these jokes don’t pack quite the same punch — because we’ve made it so much easier to care for the people we love.”

#5347. XTI Aerospace Eliminates Class B Units and Enters into Warrant Exchange Agreement, Simplifying Capital Structure

FORT LAUDERDALE, Fla., Nov. 25, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- XTI Aerospace, Inc. (Nasdaq: XTIA) ("XTI Aerospace," "XTI," or the "Company"), parent company of Drone Nerds, LLC, ("Drone Nerds"), a leading drone solutions platform serving commercial, enterprise and government customers, today announced that the Company has eliminated all outstanding Class B Units held by the sellers of Drone Nerds. In addition, the Company has entered into warrant exchange agreements, subject to customary closing conditions, with holders representing approximately 40% of its outstanding warrants, simplifying the Company's capital structure.

In a transaction dated November 18, 2026, all Class B Units of XTI Drones Holdings, LLC, a subsidiary formed in connection with XTI Aerospace's November 2025 acquisitions of Drone Nerds and Anzu Robotics, were converted into 6,524,576 shares of XTI Aerospace common stock. They were exchanged on a one-to-one basis. These securities are held directly by The Origin Group DN, Inc. and The Origin Group AZ, Inc. Following the exchange, no Class B Units remain outstanding.

The Company also announced today that it has entered into Securities Exchange Agreements with certain holders of outstanding warrants to purchase shares of the Company's common stock, par value $0.001 per share (the "Common Stock"). Pursuant to the Exchange Agreements, certain warrant holders agreed to exchange warrants exercisable for an aggregate of 8,522,052 shares of Common Stock for an aggregate of 2,840,690 newly issued shares of Common Stock. Following the Exchange, warrants to purchase approximately 12,670,129 shares of Common Stock remain outstanding.

The warrants were originally issued pursuant to the Underwriting Agreement dated June 24, 2025 between the Company and ThinkEquity LLC as representative of the several underwriters named therein, and the Placement Agency Agreement dated September 12, 2025 between the Company and ThinkEquity, and certain warrants were issued to ThinkEquity and its designees in connection with certain financings.

As a result of these transactions, XTI Aerospace now has approximately 47.8 million shares of common stock as of November 25, 2026.

"The elimination of certain legacy acquisition and financing securities marks an important step in simplifying our capital structure," said Jeremy Schneiderman, Interim CEO of XTI Aerospace. "With the removal of the Class B Units we believe we are better positioned with a solid foundation to execute on our strategic growth initiatives while enhancing shareholder value."

ThinkEquity served as financial advisor, and Blank Rome LLP and Taft Law served as legal counsel in connection with the transactions.

No Offer or SolicitationThis announcement is for informational purposes only and shall not constitute an offer to purchase or a solicitation of an offer to sell the warrants or an offer to sell or a solicitation of an offer to buy any shares of common stock in any state in which such offer, solicitation, or sale would be unlawful before registration or qualification under the laws of any such state.

XTI Aerospace, Inc. ("XTI") (Nasdaq: XTIA) is focused on building a leading platform for commercial and government drone adoption in the growing unmanned aircraft systems ("UAS") industry. Through its subsidiary, Drone Nerds, LLC, XTI supports enterprise and government customers in sectors including public safety, agriculture, construction, and energy across the drone program lifecycle, from hardware sourcing and deployment to training, service, repair, and the proprietary Always Flyingâ¢ program. Its established U.S. customer base and reputation as a trusted solutions provider position the company as a go-to-market partner for drone manufacturers and software developers seeking to scale in the domestic market.

#5346. 3 forces moving SPCX stock on Tesla merger talk that has no terms

Dilution fears, merger arbitrage and S&P 500 hopes all move SPCX stock, yet each rests on Tesla deal terms that no one has set.

Investors are trading SpaceX shares around a possible merger with Tesla $TSLA whose price and structure nobody has set. SpaceX's amended IPO filing warned that the company may sell a large amount of new stock to pay for future deals, according to CNBC, and investors have read that warning with Tesla in mind. Every trade in SPCX that turns on the merger is a bet on terms that do not yet exist.

The people closest to the deal speak warmly about the idea but have not committed to it. "There's no question that there are synergies between Tesla and SpaceX in our futures," Gwynne Shotwell, SpaceX's president and COO, told CNBC. Both companies have set up board committees to weigh a deal, yet no transaction has won the backing of either board. Elon Musk also cannot push a deal through on his own. CNBC reports that Musk has acknowledged shareholders would need to approve a merger first, and he is barred from taking part directly in the negotiations of those committees. Until that process produces terms, every number attached to a Tesla-SpaceX merger is an assumption, and investors should weigh each claim about SPCX with that in mind.

Yahoo Finance has laid out why SPCX shares have been moving amid the Tesla merger talks, from traders betting against the stock to the hope that a deal could open the door to the S&P 500. Shareholders have already paid for the uncertainty. SpaceX priced its IPO at $135 per share, according to CNBC. SPCX traded as low as $119.51 on Nov. 25 after a one-day drop of 5.01%, so anyone who got shares at the IPO price is now holding a loss. Most of the arguments for buying or selling the stock depend on the shape of a deal, meaning a price and a share swap that no one has set. Each argument is only as solid as the assumption beneath it. Some of the pressure on SPCX would remain even if no merger happened. Investors who separate the two kinds of pressure can tell which worries would likely fade once terms emerge and which would stay.

What worries SPCX holders most is not a merger itself but the number of new shares SpaceX might have to issue if it paid for Tesla $TSLA in stock. Yahoo Finance ranks that fear first among the forces weighing on the stock. Gary Black, managing partner of The Future Fund, estimated in a post on X $TWTR that a Tesla deal could mean roughly 52% more SpaceX shares. A possible acquisition of Cursor, by contrast, would dilute existing holders by 3.4% measured at the IPO valuation, according to CNBC. For anyone who holds SPCX, a Tesla deal on the scale Black describes would leave each existing share representing a much smaller part of the company.

The 52% figure describes one possible scenario, and its size depends on the inputs Black chose. His estimate assumes SpaceX pays a 25% premium for Tesla. A smaller premium would require fewer new shares, and a larger one would require more. The estimate also assumes an all-stock deal, so if SpaceX paid any part of the price in another form, it would issue fewer shares. Investors are right that a stock deal would dilute their holdings, but the size of that dilution depends on two assumptions that no one has confirmed.

The public holders who would share the dilution have little say in the company. Musk controls 82.4% of SpaceX's voting power after the IPO, according to CNBC, which leaves outside shareholders with a small share of the votes. SPCX buyers can factor the dilution risk into the price they pay, but their votes carry little weight against his.

SPCX holders should treat dilution as a cost they may have to accept rather than a decision they control.

Part of the selling in SPCX comes from SpaceX's role in the hypothetical deal, not from any judgment about its rocket business. In the merger investors are imagining, SpaceX would be the acquirer. Traders who bet on mergers buy the company being acquired and short the buyer, so SPCX lands on the side being sold whatever SpaceX's own prospects look like. Those traders keep selling SPCX until terms emerge, and no one has offered any. The selling rests on a deal structure that doesn't exist yet, and it says nothing about how SpaceX runs its business.

The traders are betting on a gap that no one can measure. The two companies haven't agreed how Tesla $TSLA stock would convert into SpaceX stock, so traders have no locked-in profit to aim for, only a guess at what the terms might turn out to be. Regulatory scrutiny could also block a SpaceX-Tesla merger, according to CNBC. Closing is expected to take at least 12 months, Yahoo Finance reports, so arbitrage traders would carry the risk of a blocked deal for at least a year even after terms appear. SPCX holders shouldn't expect the selling to end neatly once terms are announced.

Arbitrage can't explain every drop in SPCX. SpaceX shares were down about 9% one Thursday afternoon, and Tesla shares about 11%, during a broad sell-off in tech stocks, according to CNBC. Tesla fell even though arbitrage traders are buyers of its stock, and the sell-off reached well beyond the two companies, so SPCX holders lost value that day for reasons that went beyond the merger trade.

The political backdrop adds pressure that a deal wouldn't remove. "While policy is naturally hard to predict, we could envision SpaceX facing some incremental headwinds in this type of backdrop," Deutsche Bank analysts said in a note, as reported by CNBC. That kind of weakness would remain whether or not SpaceX and Tesla ever combine.

Only the arbitrage part of SPCX's slide depends on the merger's terms, and the rest is likely to stay after those terms arrive.

SPCX holders have one argument for buying rather than selling. A merger with Tesla $TSLA, already a member of the S&P 500, could put SpaceX on a fast track into the index and potentially set off buying by index funds, according to JPMorgan $JPM analysts, as reported by Yahoo Finance. The analysts describe a possible effect of a deal that no one has agreed to, so the upside can be no more real than the merger itself. Investors who expect a shortcut point to SpaceX's size, but the company that runs the index has already turned down that argument. S&P Global $SPGI said, as reported by CNBC, that "exceptions to the financial viability, seasoning, and IWF (investable weight factor) requirements should not be granted solely based on market capitalization."

SpaceX can't qualify on its own because it loses money. The company lost $4.94 billion in 2025, according to CNBC, and Art Hogan, chief market strategist at B. Riley Wealth, praises S&P for insisting that companies earn a profit before they join. That loss is why investors treat the merger as a back door. A deal could also let SpaceX skip the 12-month wait that a newly listed stock normally serves before it can join. S&P has not said how it would treat SpaceX as part of a company already in the index, so holders are betting on a ruling no one has made. A possible index lift that depends on an unapproved deal and an open rules question is a weak reason to buy SPCX today.

Index funds will have reasons to buy SpaceX that don't involve Tesla. The Nasdaq $NDAQ 100 has already changed its rules to ease entry for the largest companies, CNBC reports, and S&P plans to modify entry rules for the S&P Total Market Index and the Dow Jones U.S. Total Stock Market Index to give SpaceX a path in. S&P is holding its line only at the flagship S&P 500.

The index buying that is coming doesn't depend on Tesla, and the part that does is the least certain piece of the story.

#5344. Google acquires Seattle startup Howie and its AI scheduling assistant

Chronicling the Seattle and Pacific Northwest startup scene. SEE MORE

by Kurt Schlosser on Nov 18, 2026 at 2:03 pmNovember 18, 2026 at 2:03 pm

Google is bringing Seattle-based Howie, maker of an AI scheduling assistant that works from your inbox, into its Google Labs division.

Terms of the deal were not disclosed this week. Google Labs, the company’s experimental arm, announced the acquisition in a post on X, saying it “can’t wait to learn from them as we build the next generation of intuitive AI tools together for small businesses.”

Howie CEO and co-founder Austin Petersmith said on LinkedIn that the team will continue building Howie at Google. “Howie has always been built on top of Gmail and Google Calendar, so Google Labs is the perfect place for us to take this product to the next level,” he wrote.

Petersmith co-founded Howie around 2023 with CTO Dave Newman. The two first worked together in 2013 at Assembly, which Newman co-founded, and prototyped an AI assistant in 2015 before deciding the market wasn’t ready.

We’re excited to welcome Howie to Google Labs! The @Howie_ai team has spent years figuring out scheduling and calendar management. We can’t wait to learn from them as we build the next generation of intuitive AI tools together for small businesses 🤝 https://t.co/8bzjebeGdD

Users cc Howie on an email thread, and it coordinates meeting times, adds events to calendars, follows up as needed and flags scheduling conflicts. Customers set their own rules in an open-ended preferences document, such as “if it’s a pitch call, set it to 25 minutes and use Zoom.”

Behind the scenes, Howie ran tasks through fine-tuned language models and looped in human scheduling experts when the AI wasn’t confident.

Howie raised a $6 million seed round led by True Ventures in September 2025, when it launched publicly out of private beta. At the time, it had more than 1,000 paying customers, including startup founders, venture capitalists, recruiters, consultants and journalists, and was scheduling more than 5,000 meetings a week.

The deal comes as Google and rivals including OpenAI, Anthropic and Meta race to build AI agents that complete tasks on behalf of users. Google Labs acquired music generation platform ProducerAI earlier this year.

#5343. NFL guarantees explained, from skill and injury protection to dead money

Guaranteed money in NFL contracts comes in several forms, from signing bonuses to vesting guarantees, and this guide explains how each works and when teams can void it

An NFL contract has two numbers that matter. One is the total value announced on signing day. The other is the portion a player is certain to collect. Those figures are often far apart. The gap between them shapes how teams build rosters, manage the salary cap and decide when to move on from a player.

Most NFL contracts are not guaranteed in full. A team can release a player and owe him nothing beyond the guaranteed portion of his deal. That makes guaranteed money in NFL contracts the clearer measure of what a deal is worth to the player. It is also the clearer measure of how much risk a team has taken on.

Guarantees are not a single category. Some money is protected only if a player is injured on the job. Some is protected against a release for performance reasons or for salary-cap reasons. Some is protected against all of those at once. That is what "fully guaranteed" means. Money can also change status over time. It can start with limited protection and become fully guaranteed on a set date.

The signing bonus sits at the center of many deals. It is guaranteed to the player. The team, however, spreads its cap charge evenly across the contract, up to a maximum of five years. That accounting choice shapes much of what happens later. It feeds into dead money, the cap charges that remain after a player is released or traded. It also explains why teams use the post-June 1 designation. And it explains why some contracts include void years that a player is not expected to play.

Guarantees also have limits. Offset language can reduce what a former team owes once a released player signs elsewhere. A team can also try to void guarantees or recover bonus money when a player breaches his contract. Failing to report, retiring and being suspended are examples. Whether that effort succeeds depends on the contract's language and the collective bargaining agreement between the league and the players' union. Sometimes it depends on an arbitrator.

Most of the money in an NFL contract is not guaranteed. A team can release a player and owe him nothing beyond the guaranteed portion of his deal, however many years or dollars remain on paper.

That makes the announced value a best-case figure rather than a promise. A deal is usually reported with a length and a total. That total assumes the player stays on the roster for every season of the contract.

If the team cuts him early, the unguaranteed salary in the remaining years is never paid. The player keeps only what the team committed to in advance. Everything above that amount depends on the club's ongoing decision to keep employing him.

The guaranteed figure is the part of the deal a player can count on. It is owed whether or not he finishes the contract. The unguaranteed remainder works more like a series of future choices the team can make or decline.

Guaranteed money can take more than one form. A signing bonus is guaranteed to the player. Salary for a given season can also be guaranteed, either fully or only against specific risks such as injury.

This explains why two contracts with similar totals can mean very different things for the people who sign them. One deal may protect a large share of its value. Another may protect only a small slice, leaving most of the reported total tied to future roster decisions.

The split matters to teams as well. Unguaranteed money disappears when a player is released. The guaranteed portion is the commitment a club cannot walk away from. Releasing a player saves a team only the unguaranteed part of his remaining pay.

The guaranteed amount, not the total, shows how secure a player's pay is. How much is guaranteed, in what form and from which date are the details that decide what a player collects.

A signing bonus is guaranteed money that an NFL player is owed for agreeing to a contract. For salary-cap purposes, the league does not count it all at once. The bonus is spread evenly over the years of the deal, up to a maximum of five years.

That even split is called proration. Each season covered by the deal carries an equal share of the bonus on the team's books. The share does not change based on how the player performs or how many games he plays. Because the shares are fixed at signing, a team knows the bonus charge for every season of the deal in advance.

The five-year ceiling shapes how longer contracts are counted. On a three-year deal, the bonus is divided into three equal parts. On a five-year deal, it is divided into five. On a deal that runs longer than five years, the bonus is still split over just five seasons. The seasons beyond that carry none of it.

Proration is an accounting rule, not a payment schedule. It governs how the bonus counts against the cap. It does not determine when the money reaches the player. The timing of the actual payments is a separate matter set by the contract.

That separation lets a team commit a large sum to a player while counting only a fraction of it against the cap in any single season. The bonus can keep appearing on the cap sheet in seasons after the cash has already been paid.

For the player, the value lies in the guarantee. A signing bonus belongs to the protected part of a deal, not the part a team can walk away from by releasing him.

That sets it apart from much of a contract's headline value. Salary scheduled for later seasons may never be paid if the player is released first. A release does not cancel the signing bonus.

The size of the bonus also affects how much of a deal is protected. A contract built around a large signing bonus and modest yearly salaries puts more of its value into guaranteed money. A deal with a small bonus leaves more of its value exposed to an early release.

NFL guarantees come in three main types, and each covers a different reason a team might cut a player. A skill guarantee protects against release for performance, an injury guarantee protects a player hurt on the job, and a cap guarantee protects a player released for salary-cap reasons.

The skill guarantee covers a judgment about ability. If a club releases a player because it decides he is no longer good enough, a skill guarantee means it still owes the protected amount. The decision to move on does not cancel the obligation.

The injury guarantee is tied to a specific event. It applies when a player is hurt while performing his job for the team. If that injury leads to his release, the guaranteed salary remains payable. It does not shield him from a release driven by declining play or by budget pressure.

The cap guarantee covers a third scenario. Teams operate under a salary cap, and a club sometimes cuts a player to clear room for other spending. A cap guarantee means that reason alone does not let the team walk away from the protected money.

These categories are separate promises. A contract can include any combination of the three. Some deals protect money against only one risk, while others stack two or all three on the same salary.

A single guaranteed total does not show which protection applies to each dollar. Money shielded only against injury gives a healthy player little security if his performance slips. Money with only a cap guarantee does not help him if the team cuts him for poor play.

Each protection is defined by the reason for ending the deal. That makes the reason for a release central to what the player collects. Two players cut on the same day for the same reason can leave with very different sums, depending on which protections their contracts carry.

Reading guarantee language comes down to two questions: how much money is protected, and against which of the three risks.

A fully guaranteed contract protects a player's money against every standard reason a team might stop paying. Those reasons are release for performance, an injury suffered on the job and a cut made for salary-cap purposes.

When that protection is in place at signing, the team is committed to the full amount from the first day. No later date or condition has to pass before the money is secure.

Most NFL deals work differently. A typical contract guarantees only part of its value. The team can release the player and owe nothing beyond that part. Some contracts also carry one type of guarantee without the others. A player might be covered if he is hurt on the job but not if he is cut for performance.

A fully guaranteed contract closes those gaps. Releasing the player does not erase what he is owed. Poor play, an injury or a tight salary cap does not change the total either.

Kirk Cousins signed one of these deals with the Minnesota Vikings in 2018. It was a three-year contract worth $84 million, and the entire amount was fully guaranteed.

Deshaun Watson's 2022 contract with the Cleveland Browns followed the same structure on a larger scale. It covered five years and $230 million, all of it fully guaranteed.

Full guarantees also appear at the start of some careers. First-round rookie contracts are typically fully guaranteed. A team that drafts a player in the first round is usually committed to his whole rookie deal from the day he signs it.

Players drafted in later rounds face a different arrangement. Their contracts more often guarantee only the signing bonus. The rest of their salary is not protected. A team can release them and owe nothing beyond that bonus.

The split between those two groups ties financial security to draft position. A first-round pick usually holds a fully guaranteed deal from signing. A later-round pick often keeps each season's salary only by staying on the roster.

A vesting date is the point at which a limited guarantee becomes a full one. Some contract guarantees protect a salary against injury only at first, then become fully guaranteed on a set date, usually tied to the start of the league year.

Before that date, the protection is narrow. An injury-only guarantee covers a player who gets hurt on the job. It does not cover a release for performance or for salary-cap reasons. A healthy player cut ahead of the vesting date can leave without that money.

After the date passes, the same salary is protected against all three of those risks. The team owes it whether the player is cut for skill, for injury or to clear cap space. The dollar amount does not change on the vesting date. What changes is the set of circumstances in which the team must pay it.

That structure turns the vesting date into a decision point. A team that wants to move on from a player has a reason to act before the guarantee locks in. A team that keeps the player past that date has, in effect, committed to the salary. For the player, the date marks when an expected payment becomes one he can count on.

The fifth-year option on a first-round pick follows this pattern. When a team exercises the option, the salary for that extra season is guaranteed for injury only. It becomes fully guaranteed on the first day of the league year. Until then, the team keeps some flexibility over a player it has already chosen to retain.

The franchise tag works differently. There is no waiting period tied to the calendar. Franchise-tag salary becomes fully guaranteed once the player signs the tender. The trigger is the player's signature, not a date on the league schedule.

Vesting language also explains why a guaranteed total announced at signing can overstate what is secure on day one. That figure may include money protected only against injury. Checking when each portion vests shows how much is secure immediately and how much becomes secure later.

Dead money is the salary cap charge a team still carries for a player who is no longer on its roster. It is made up of guaranteed money and unamortized bonus money that remain on the cap after a release or trade.

Bonus money turns into dead money because of a gap between when it is paid and when it is counted. The player collects the bonus, but the team books its cap charge in yearly installments. If he leaves before every installment has been counted, the remaining ones do not vanish. They still have to land on the cap.

Guaranteed salary follows the same logic. If a contract protects a player's pay for a future season and the team cuts him, the club still owes that money. The amount counts against the cap even though the player will never take another snap for the team.

Non-guaranteed salary works differently. A released player's unprotected base salary comes off the books entirely, and it never becomes dead money. Only protected or already-paid money can leave a charge behind.

A trade can leave dead money behind as well. The original team has already paid the signing bonus. The share of that bonus not yet counted stays on its cap after the player moves to his new club.

This math shapes roster decisions. A release frees only the difference between what the player would have counted and the dead money he leaves behind. When the dead charge is large, a cut can save little cap room that season. In some cases it uses more cap space than keeping the player would have.

Dead money cannot be shifted to another team or wiped off the books. It occupies cap space the team cannot spend on anyone else. A club carrying heavy dead charges has less room to sign free agents or extend its own players.

Timing matters too. A separate tool, the post-June 1 designation, changes how the charge is divided across seasons.

An NFL team can designate up to two player releases as post-June 1 cuts. That label spreads the dead money from each of those releases across two seasons instead of loading it into one.

Dead money is the cap charge a team still carries after a player leaves through a release or trade. It can include guaranteed salary the team still owes and bonus money it has not yet counted against the cap. The player is off the roster, but the charge remains.

The designation changes timing, not size. A released player is still owed every guaranteed dollar his contract promises. The label does not cut his pay, cancel a bonus or reduce what the team must pay him. It moves part of the cap accounting from one season into the next.

The salary cap limits what a team can spend on player pay in a season. A large dead-money charge in one year uses cap space that could otherwise go to other players. Splitting the charge across two seasons lowers the burden in the first one.

The cost is deferred, not avoided. Whatever leaves the first season lands in the second. A team that uses the designation accepts a smaller dead-money charge now in exchange for an added charge the following year.

Bonus proration explains why the split can be large. A signing bonus is guaranteed money for the player, but its cap cost is counted in pieces over the life of the deal. A player released early in a long contract can leave several seasons of uncounted bonus behind. The designation lets a team divide that leftover amount between two seasons rather than absorbing it at once.

The limit of two designations forces a choice. A team weighing several releases must decide which ones gain the most from the split. Releases that leave behind the largest dead-money charges free the most room in the first season.

Void years are placeholder seasons added to the end of an NFL contract for one reason: to stretch how a bonus is counted against the salary cap. The player is not expected to play them.

The tool builds on signing bonus accounting. A bonus is charged to the cap in equal shares across a contract's years, with proration capped at five years.

Void years work inside that rule. Each added season counts as a contract year for proration purposes. More years on paper means the bonus is divided into more shares. Each share is smaller. The bonus charge in every season the player actually plays shrinks as a result.

That is the point of the structure. A team carries a lower cap figure while the player is on its roster. The rest of the cost is pushed into seasons when he will not be there.

The five-year ceiling still limits the math. Void years can stretch proration only as far as that ceiling allows. A deal that already runs five real seasons gains no extra bonus spreading from added years.

The deferred charge comes due when the contract voids. At that point, the bonus shares assigned to the placeholder seasons have not yet counted. They accelerate onto the cap together rather than spreading over the years they were assigned to.

The same acceleration applies if the team releases or trades the player before the contract reaches its void date. Any bonus shares not yet counted, including those tied to void years, stay on the cap as dead money.

Void years do not change what the player is owed. The signing bonus is guaranteed money either way. The added seasons alter only when its cap charge is recorded, not whether the player collects it.

A void year also differs from an ordinary final season, which a player is under contract to play. It exists on paper for cap accounting, not for games.

Offset language lets a team that releases a player subtract whatever he earns from a new team from the guaranteed money it still owes him. The clause turns the old team's obligation into a backstop rather than a separate paycheck.

The clause only matters after a release. Offset language applies to the guaranteed money a team still owes at that point. It does not create a guarantee, and it does not erase one. It changes how much of the remaining guarantee the former team ends up paying.

The mechanism is subtraction. The former team starts with the guaranteed amount left on the contract. It then deducts what the player earns from his new club. The former team pays whatever is left over.

The effect depends on the size of the new contract. A player who signs a small deal elsewhere reduces the old team's bill only slightly. A player whose new earnings match or exceed the remaining guarantee can reduce that bill to nothing. In the first case, his combined pay from the two clubs equals the guarantee he was already owed. In the second, it equals his new salary.

Without an offset clause, the arithmetic runs the other way. The former team pays the full remaining guarantee regardless of what happens next. The player keeps that money and also collects whatever his new team pays him. That outcome is commonly called double-dipping.

The presence or absence of an offset therefore changes what a guarantee is worth in practice. Two contracts with identical guaranteed totals can produce different payouts after a release. The deciding factor is whether the former club is allowed to count the player's new earnings against what it owes.

Offsets also shape the money a released player can expect from his next deal. With an offset in place, the guarantee from his old team already sets a floor on his income. A new contract below that floor shifts who pays him, not how much he receives.

An NFL team can generally seek to void guarantees or recover bonus money when a player breaches his contract. Failing to report, retiring and being suspended are among the breaches that can open that door.

A guarantee is a promise from the team, but it rests on the player meeting his own obligations under the deal. When a player stops meeting them, the team can argue that its side of the promise no longer holds.

That is why a guarantee is not unconditional. Its protections cover a release for performance, injury or salary-cap reasons. A breach by the player is a separate matter.

Failing to report is one example. A player who holds out from training camp or skips mandatory team activities is not providing the services his contract calls for. That absence can give the team grounds to challenge money it agreed to guarantee.

Retirement is a different kind of breach. Here the player chooses to stop playing before his contract runs out. A team in that position can seek to void the guarantees that remain. It can also try to recover signing bonus money it has already paid.

Suspension is a third trigger. A suspended player is unavailable to his team for the games he misses. That absence can give the team grounds to seek to void guarantees.

None of these outcomes is automatic. Whether a team can actually void a guarantee or recoup a bonus turns on three factors. The first is the specific language in the player's contract. The second is the collective bargaining agreement between the NFL and the NFL Players Association. The third, in some disputes, is the ruling of an arbitrator.

Contract language matters because guarantees are negotiated deal by deal. One contract may spell out exactly which conduct cancels a guarantee. Another may be written more narrowly, leaving the team fewer grounds to act.

The collective bargaining agreement sets rules that individual contracts must follow. It shapes what a team may pursue against a player and how disagreements over money are handled.

When the team and the player read those documents differently, the dispute can go to arbitration. An arbitrator then decides whether a breach occurred. The arbitrator also decides what money, if any, the team can withhold or claim back.

#5342. Zeno Power makes progress on an underwater power system that will eventually go nuclear

by Alan Boyle on Nov 19, 2026 at 7:00 amNovember 19, 2026 at 8:01 am

Zeno Power has hit a major milestone in its push to build nuclear batteries for underwater use.

The startup said today that it successfully demonstrated an electrically heated Stirling generator in a controlled maritime setting in Washington state. The two-week demonstration produced electrical power outputs in excess of 20 watts, said Lindsey Boles, Zeno’s chief product officer.

“It’s a really big step for us — just solidifying our expertise in how to design these, and then confirming our ability to translate that into operational hardware that meets or exceeds what our customers need,” Boles told GeekWire.

Zeno is developing the power system with support from the Department of Defense as a follow-up to an initial $7.5 million contract awarded in 2023. The generator uses a Stirling engine to convert heat into electricity by cycling gas through heating and cooling phases in a closed cylinder.

For the recent demonstration, the prototype device relied on an electric heating element. Future devices will instead rely on heat generated by the radioactive decay of strontium-90, a radioisotope that can be extracted from spent nuclear fuel.

Nuclear batteries have been in use for decades, primarily for space missions ranging from the Apollo moon shots to NASA’s Voyager spacecraft and Mars rovers. But the batteries being developed by Zeno Power promise to be at least four times more efficient than traditional radioisotope thermoelectric generators, Boles said.

Boles said the non-radiological test exceeded expectations. “There’s a difference between a design that works on paper and hardware that works in the field,” she said in a news release. “This is the moment our team has been building toward: proof that this technology works outside the lab.”

Long-lasting nuclear batteries could be used to power undersea sensor networks or recharge autonomous underwater vehicles. “There are a lot of applications, especially on the maritime front, that we really want electricity for,” Boles said. “And we really don’t need a ton of it. But we need it to be really reliable, and we need it to be long endurance, and we need it to be self-managed. … I think of it like a slow Tesla supercharger on the seabed.”

Retired Navy Adm. John Richardson, former chief of naval operations and a member of Zeno’s board of directors, called the recent test an “important step toward undersea superiority.”

“Protecting maritime infrastructure and powering distributed systems at sea requires energy; energy that lasts for years, not days or months,” Richardson said in a written statement. “As competition intensifies in contested domains, powered subsea systems will help keep us ahead. Zeno Power has steadily reduced risk, proven its technology, built a supply chain, and prepared to scale production.”

Next year, Zeno Power plans to install a radioisotope heat source in its generator and test the system in a water tank under controlled laboratory conditions. If those tests are successful, Zeno will move forward with the first operational seabed deployment of its radioisotope-fueled maritime system later in 2027.

The maritime battery isn’t Zeno’s only product. The company is also working on a nuclear-powered heater system for spacecraft, with a demonstration on the lunar surface planned as early as 2028. Zeno’s broader vision is to provide long-lasting, reliable power on the moon and Mars, and in extreme environments on Earth.

Since its founding in 2018, Zeno has secured $105 million in private capital and has brought in $60 million in contracts with the Pentagon and NASA. The company has more than 95 employees at locations in Seattle, California and Washington, D.C., with the largest contingent working at its engineering headquarters in Seattle’s South Lake Union district.

#5341. GenScript Convenes AI, Biotech and Investment Leaders in London as Faster AI-Enabled Drug Design Raises the Stakes for Biological Evidence

Industry leaders point to better data, faster learning cycles and closer connections between computation and experimentation as critical to translating AI-designed molecules into development decisions

LONDON, Nov. 25, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- AI drug discovery is shifting from a race to design faster to a race to learn faster. As AI expands the speed and scale of design, the advantage increasingly lies with those who can turn those designs into validated biological evidence that informs decisions and improves models.

GenScript highlights how biological evidence and faster learning are becoming critical as AI accelerates drug design.

That was the central proposition GenScript Biotech Corporation put to leaders from pharma, AI-native biotechnology, investment and science funding at the 2026 GenScript Biotech Global Forum London. Held during the week of the Jefferies London Healthcare Conference under the theme "AI, Biotech & Capital," the forum brought together executives from Eli Lilly and Company, Latent Labs, Sofinnova Partners, Basecamp Research, ARIA and GenScript to explore where AI is already creating scientific and economic value, where biology remains a limiting factor, and what evidence will be required as AI-generated possibilities move closer to development.

From AI Possibility to Biological Evidence

Panelists included Alan Belicha, PhD, Senior Director, Ecosystem Growth and Contributor Partnerships at Eli Lilly and Company; Simon Kohl, PhD, Founder and CEO of Latent Labs; Edward Kliphuis, Partner at Sofinnova Partners; Richard Pearce, Chief Business Officer at Basecamp Research; and Maximilian Sichrovsky, PhD, Science & Technology Lead at ARIA. GenScript was represented by Ray Chen, PhD, President of GenScript Life Science Group; Zhenyan Yan, PhD, Vice President of Corporate Development & Strategy; and Aylin Kosova Bilgin, Chief Marketing and Corporate Communications Officer.

Their discussion highlighted three forces shaping the next phase of AI-enabled drug discovery:

AI is moving into harder biology. Kohl described how quickly AI-enabled protein design is evolving, with the field moving beyond binding toward more complex modalities and questions of developability. Even with that progress, he said, the critical gap lies between generating a promising binder and developing a candidate a company is prepared to advance toward the clinic. Closing it requires addressing biological properties that are harder to model and more difficult to characterize experimentally. "This is all about building AI platforms that advance our partners' portfolios, our partners' programs," added Kohl. "Increasingly, we're betting on both building generative models and the agents around them to create end-to-end workflows. I think that's the exciting moment in time. It feels a lot like what GPT-3 felt like in language. That's what this field is now undergoing, and we couldn't be more excited for what's to come over the next one to two years."

Data quality and biological relevance are becoming more important. Panelists pointed to two related gaps: the need for datasets that support biologically relevant predictions, rather than simply more data, and the need for people who can bridge AI and wet-lab biology. As models take on harder biological questions, closer connections between dataset design, experimentation and computation will be critical to generating evidence that improves predictions and informs development decisions.

Capital follows evidence, not design volume. Pearce noted that AI is becoming effective at specific discovery tasks and could allow companies to reach the clinic with less capital than a traditional biotech would need. Long-term value, however, will depend on whether promising molecules can progress beyond design and through development, where biological and ultimately clinical evidence determines which ones move forward. As candidate generation accelerates, the evidence behind each candidate becomes more consequential in determining where development resources and capital are committed. "Ultimately, we're all paying for healthcare, and healthcare costs keep going up. And most development costs are actually going toward drugs that fail; the industry needs to think differently so that environment can change," Pearce added. "I think we're at the point where, with a better understanding of patient biology and stratification, new business models will evolve. Compared to other industries that have changed business models, the pharma industry is still doing the same thing it did 70 years ago: discovering a compound, doing a clinical trial, and hoping it works. In 20 years' time, I think that will have changed â and we will know that a new therapy works for a specific individual."

Turning Faster Design into Faster Learning

For GenScript, these themes converge around learning velocity: connecting AI-driven design with synthesis, expression, biological testing and usable data to shorten the path from computational possibility to experimental evidence. As discovery cycles accelerate, researchers also need the scientific depth and biological context to interpret that evidence and make informed development decisions.

The shift is already reflected in GenScript's AI drug discovery (AIDD) business, which doubled year over year to $37.8 million in revenue in the first half of 2026. As AI-native companies and pharmaceutical teams move toward larger experimental cycles and more extensive biological characterization, the need for high-quality experimental evidence is growing.

"The data we generate has two important purposes: to help advance promising candidates and to feed what we learn back into the next cycle," said Chen. "As AI allows us to explore more targets, modalities and deeper biology, generating decision-ready data becomes even more important. AI advances discovery. Biology advances AI. GenScript powers the cycle."

The GenScript Biotech Global Forum is GenScript's thought-leadership platform for bringing together leaders across science, technology, biotechnology and investment to examine the trends reshaping life sciences innovation.

"This conversation doesn't stop in London," added Chen. "We'll continue it in San Francisco during JPM Week because the questions ahead are bigger than any one company or discipline. Progress will depend on how effectively AI, biology and capital come together to accelerate learning and translate scientific possibility into better medicines."

#5340. Amazon’s $18B bet on Anthropic tops $200B, for a moment, in the Claude maker’s historic market debut

by Todd Bishop on Nov 19, 2026 at 9:54 amNovember 19, 2026 at 10:10 am

Anthropic made its Nasdaq debut today in a record $81.3 billion initial public offering, with big financial stakes for the Seattle area’s two tech giants.

For Amazon, the IPO is a paper windfall. The company started putting money into Anthropic in 2023, about $18 billion in all. At the $83 IPO price, its stake was worth about $161 billion. With Anthropic opening at $111.50 a share, that number was closer to $216 billion. The stock has since dropped below $100, which put Amazon’s stake under $200 billion.

Beyond the value of the investment, Anthropic is a major customer for Amazon’s cloud platform. The Claude maker has committed to spend at least $110 billion on Amazon Web Services through 2036.

For Microsoft, it’s more complicated. The Redmond company agreed in late 2025 to invest up to $5 billion but hasn’t disclosed the size of its stake. Microsoft is buying $1 billion of Anthropic stock alongside the IPO, one of seven tech companies buying a combined $26 billion. Anthropic has committed to spend at least $47 billion on Microsoft’s Azure cloud through 2033.

But Microsoft is also pitching its own AI models against Anthropic’s, and it has been working to replace Anthropic’s models with OpenAI’s in some Copilot features, The Information reported this week.

Listing Anthropic’s compute partners on CNBC this morning, co-founder Daniela Amodei named Nvidia, Amazon, Google and Broadcom, but not Microsoft. Whether it was a slip or something more significant, it was an interesting omission.

A historic debut: The offering tops SpaceX’s $75 billion IPO in June, and it makes Anthropic the first standalone AI lab to go public, ahead of OpenAI.

The five-year-old company was valued at about $1.5 trillion at the $83 IPO price, on a fully diluted basis that counts employee stock and other shares not yet issued. The stock opened at $111.50, valuing Anthropic at about $2 trillion on the same basis. It has since traded as low as about $95.

Speaking before the opening bell, CEO Dario Amodei said Anthropic will slow the training and release of its AI models for as long as it takes to be confident they’re safe, and that going public only strengthens that resolve.

“We will not bend to either business nor political pressure,” he said.

In an interview with CNBC’s Andrew Ross Sorkin afterward, Amodei called the push and pull between growth and that kind of restraint “one of the central tensions at the heart of the company.”

Anthropic is also a public benefit corporation, a structure that legally requires the company to balance shareholders’ interests with the public good.

What’s next: Both Seattle-area giants have hedged their bets. Microsoft owns about 24% of OpenAI, and Amazon put $50 billion into OpenAI earlier this year.

OpenAI, which confidentially filed for its own IPO in June, is still aiming to go public in 2027.

Anthropic’s co-founders and some of its biggest shareholders are barred from selling for up to a year under the IPO’s lock-up rules, and Amazon has said it expects a customary lock-up period.

Amazon will update the value of its Anthropic holdings in its fourth-quarter results, much of it through earnings, which means the paper windfall is likely to boost Amazon’s fourth-quarter profit even though it hasn’t sold a share.
