#5338. Why hiring neurodivergent talent isn’t enough, and what leaders should do instead

Many neuroinclusion strategies still depend on employees disclosing a diagnosis. Jonathan Mok argues support should be built into how organizations operate.

This article has been reviewed by the Quartz editorial team. The content may be licensed for reuse.

Companies are increasingly recognizing the value of neurodivergent talent, but hiring is only part of the picture. Many neuroinclusion strategies still rely on employees to disclose their diagnoses and request workplace adjustments themselves, an approach that assumes they feel safe doing so. According to a 2026 survey by the nonprofit Understood.org, about 70% of neurodivergent employees in the U.S. worry that disclosing their neurodivergence could negatively affect them at work. When employees stay silent, employers may never learn which barriers need addressing.

Jonathan Mok, a Hong Kong-based neurodiversity advocate, speaker, and leadership trainer, has seen that gap from both sides. He was diagnosed with ADHD and autism at 37, after years of working in education in Hong Kong. Today, he trains corporate teams across Asia on neuroinclusion and coaches executives who have received late diagnoses. His own experience suggests that even when employees do disclose, formal support does not always translate into belonging.

After his diagnosis, a workplace medical committee recommended that Mok should not feel obliged to attend department social gatherings. When his boss invited the team to a New Year lunch and he raised his hand to join, colleagues kept telling him nobody was forcing him to go. They meant well, but a measure intended to protect him left him feeling excluded. “I wanted to go. My boss was paying for lunch,” Mok recalls. “But the message I kept hearing was that I didn’t really belong there.”

Despite receiving formal accommodations, Mok continued to face challenges at work, and he resigned in 2020. His experience reflects a wider pattern. In a 2025 report by Boston Consulting Group, supported by SG Enable, 62% of neurodivergent employees surveyed in Singapore said their neurodivergence had been misunderstood as a poor attitude. While 99% believed reasonable accommodations would help, only 33% said these were available at their workplace, and just 24% considered them adequate.

The findings point to a disconnect between recognizing neurodivergent talent and creating the conditions for it to thrive. Gartner predicted in 2023 that by 2027, a quarter of Fortune 500 companies would actively recruit neurodivergent talent to improve business performance. Recruitment, however, is only the first step. Inclusion also depends on whether employees feel they belong, can speak up without fear of judgment, and receive support that works in practice.

Mok believes that an emphasis on meritocracy can lead some employers to assume that anyone capable enough to be hired does not need to disclose anything. Employees, in turn, try to fit in until they no longer can. He adds that organizations often focus on deficits and rely heavily on medical guidance rather than on what individuals actually want or need. In his view, support should not depend on employees asking for it; it should be built into how the organization operates.

He also challenges the idea that organizations must be ready to hire neurodivergent employees before taking any steps toward inclusion. One cosmetics retailer found that quiet shopping hours did little to ease the sensory demands of a busy store. After consulting Mok, a colleague, and store staff, it introduced ribbon-marked baskets that let customers signal a preference for minimal interaction without explaining their needs. Because retail turnover is high, the accompanying staff training was kept simple enough to pass on to new employees.

Mok points to a neurodivergent internship program at the Hong Kong office of an international insurer as a more comprehensive example. Rather than treating recruitment as the endpoint, the company paired the program with manager training and structured onboarding, helping teams build the skills to support neurodivergent colleagues. It also works with a local nonprofit organization to source talent and provide training.

To help organizations turn good intentions into action, Mok uses a 4P framework covering People, Place, Policy, and Program. It is designed as an ongoing approach rather than a one-time training session. Under People, he encourages organizations to recognize inclusive managers, create safe channels for raising concerns, and highlight neurodivergent role models. Under Place, he recommends sensory-friendly workspaces and normalizing tools that allow people to work in ways that suit them.

Policy involves clear procedures around disclosure, workplace adjustments, and job expectations, so that employees and managers know what support is available. Many managers, Mok notes, only look for guidance after a problem arises and then have to dig through documents that can run 50 or 60 pages. The program focuses on long-term planning, consultation, and partnerships with community organizations, including neurodivergent individuals and their families, so that initiatives address real needs rather than assumptions.

For companies operating across Asia, Mok stresses the importance of understanding how culture, law, and local knowledge shape neurodiversity in each market. Even within the region, conditions such as autism and ADHD are recognized differently, as the contrast between Hong Kong and mainland China shows. Such differences can complicate standardized inclusion policies. He also believes that meaningful progress is possible for organizations of every size, not only multinational corporations.

For Mok, the next stage of neuroinclusion means looking past whether organizations are willing to hire neurodivergent people and asking whether their cultures, policies, and leadership allow those employees to stay and succeed. “The next diversity metric should not be hires,” he says. “It should be stays.” A seat at the New Year lunch, offered without hesitation, may say more about an organization’s inclusion than any recruitment target.

#5337. Uncommon Thinkers: Andrew Redd’s audacious plan to turn ocean volcanoes into power plants

by Lisa Stiffler on Nov 19, 2026 at 10:07 amNovember 24, 2026 at 9:53 am

Editor’s note: This series profiles five Seattle-area “Uncommon Thinkers,” who will be recognized Dec. 10 at the GeekWire Gala in partnership with Greater Seattle Partners.

Andrew Redd‘s career path creates a tidy narrative: grow up in Seattle steeped in aviation and maritime culture, study mechanical engineering and aerospace, work at SpaceX, then launch an offshore geothermal energy startup.

The dots connect, but the picture they form is anything but ordinary: bold in vision, fast in execution and enormous in potential.

Redd has next-level ambition, and he’s directing it at solving one of the world’s biggest and most urgent problems — adding renewable, massively scalable energy that can outcompete fossil fuels and reach the grid quickly enough to make a difference in the race against climate change.

Underwater geothermal energy has never been tapped in a significant way, but to Redd, the idea was irresistible. “It checks all of the boxes for our perfect future energy source,” he said.

He founded Endurance Energy on the north shore of Seattle’s Lake Union in January 2025, and this September the team oversaw its fifth deep-sea deployment. At a site 300 miles off the Oregon coast, its prototype system generated more electricity than it consumed. The startup has raised $63 million from investors and has roughly three dozen employees.

Nate Bek, a principal at Ascend, praised Redd’s ability to attract “brilliant” talent in pursuit of his goal. The Seattle venture firm is one of the startup’s early backers.

“I’ve been deeply inspired by what [Redd]’s building at Endurance and haven’t shut up about it since the day we met,” Bek said. “He somehow makes powering the world from the bottom of the ocean feel inevitable, all while remaining remarkably measured and transparent about the progress.”

For Redd, studying engineering and aerospace in college was so clear-cut that it wasn’t a choice at all. Growing up around Boeing, seaplanes, the Museum of Flight and the Pacific Northwest’s rich maritime industry naturally pointed him toward those sectors. He wanted a degree as expansive as his influences.

“I didn’t really want to have to choose whether it was going to be boats or space travel or airplanes,” he said. “I just wanted to be able to do anything — keep the world as wide open as possible.”

After graduating from Princeton University, Redd worked at Neuralink, an Elon Musk company developing technology that lets the brain communicate directly with computers. A year later, in 2021, he moved to Musk’s rocket company, SpaceX.

That was another no-duh decision, as Redd viewed it.

“I saw SpaceX as really the place to be, where early-career people are given the most amount of resources and responsibility, and that felt like the fastest way to learn and the most engaging possible scenario to be in,” Redd said. “I wanted to be tossed into something that was a little bit crazy.”

Redd joined as SpaceX was starting to build its first orbital Starship rockets. The program brought together passionate young people and experienced SpaceX engineers who served as mentors. Wild ideas were entertained and explored. Everyone was committed to the mission. It was just the experience Redd wanted, and he planned to stick around for seven to 10 years.

Then artificial intelligence started booming.

In 2024, the build-out of sprawling, energy-hungry data centers for AI was accelerating with no end in sight. At the same time, efforts to electrify transportation, heating and cooling were driving up demand for power. Redd saw these trends sparking a surge in new natural gas generation, locking in decades of carbon emissions.

He wanted to find a better way. He went into engineering mode, focusing on all the essential criteria for an energy source: it had to be clean, not dependent on intermittent sun or wind, capable of producing massive amounts of energy, readily deployable, subject to fewer regulatory hurdles than something like nuclear, economically competitive, and scalable.

Redd recognized the tremendous heat contained under Earth’s surface as a terrific source for renewable energy and realized that most of the world’s active volcanoes are offshore. The unknown was whether the rocky ocean floor would be suitable for geothermal wells, so he did some research and found publications from geology experts who said the conditions would be “perfect.”

“You can tell,” he said, “when there’s a moment in time that you need to go and reach out and grab something, and that was really my impression — if I didn’t start this now, this would never come into existence, or wouldn’t come into existence soon enough to make a meaningful impact.”

In launching Endurance, Redd was intentional about the culture he wanted to create. He was aiming for a multidisciplinary group of mission-driven employees eager to collaborate and learn from each other: top talent that would attract more of the same and make Endurance a place people were excited to work.

“The hardest part of an early-stage startup is recruiting,” Redd said, “especially if you’re a first-time founder.”

The startup employs about a dozen SpaceX alumni, plus employees from the fusion company Helion Energy and the aerospace venture Blue Origin.

A strong team is key to Endurance’s success. That’s because, enthusiasm and passion aside, the startup faces steep engineering and economic challenges. The technology must withstand high pressure, corrosive conditions and mineral scaling inside devices, and seafloor machinery could be costly to repair. The systems will need expensive subsea cables to carry power to shore over potentially long distances. It’s a heavy lift.

While the September sea trial didn’t go perfectly, Redd is happy with the results. The company landed its 3-ton power plant on the seafloor near a natural vent and produced net energy from it — albeit for only 8.7 seconds. Technical difficulties and a power-cable failure cut the dive short.

Team members successfully operated the system remotely from Seattle through a fiber-optic network running along the seabed. Redd said he’s grateful for access to the network, which is part of the National Science Foundation’s Regional Cabled Array and operated by the University of Washington.

Endurance engineers also drilled what they called the world’s first subsea geothermal well at a site about 5,000 feet below the ocean’s surface. The 2-inch-wide, 52-foot-deep well delivered hydrothermal fluid, but the flow was too restricted to run the power plant, sending the team to the natural vent.

Redd said there’s a lot of work ahead, but the team “made huge strides” in learning and in reducing the project’s risks.

The company now is developing Leopard, its 2-megawatt generator. After testing the technology at the research site off the Oregon coast, Endurance aims to deliver power from a Leopard system in Tonga next year as its first commercial project. Subsea geothermal energy could ultimately reduce the island nation’s reliance on imported diesel and put the startup one step closer to its objective of generating terawatts of planet-friendly energy.

“This was always the end goal,” Redd said. “Create something that is highly meaningful for the world.”

Bitcoin road back toward $80,000 may have a new catalyst after news from US regulators. CFTC has opened another door for crypto inside traditional financial markets. CFTC says regulated derivatives exchanges and clearinghouses can count Bitcoin toward certain financial requirements. But what does this mean?

The guidance could help firms hold onto their Bitcoin instead of selling it to satisfy reserve requirements. It undoubtedly changes how regulated institutions can use BTC. This news comes as Bitcoin looks for reasons to reverse its recent weakness.

CFTC ALLOWS EXCHANGES COUNT BITCOIN FOR OPERATING COSTS.🚨 THIS IS HUGE !!!👉 Bitcoin enters clearinghouse reserves. pic.twitter.com/vP0NyuwLU3

Released yesterday, it allows eligible firms to use Bitcoin, Ether, and qualifying payment stablecoins toward resources covering 12 months of operating costs. BTC and ETH face a minimum 20% haircut, while qualifying stablecoins face just 2%.

Bitcoin still has plenty of ground to recover, but can this news reverse the current bleeding trajectory?

Discover: The Crypto Presales This Q4 2026

Under the guidance, regulated derivatives exchanges, swap facilities, and clearinghouses can include certain crypto holdings in their financial-resource calculations. A firm holding $1 million in Bitcoin could count $800,000 after the minimum haircut.

The allowance comes with a catch: crypto cannot satisfy the separate requirement for cash or highly liquid securities. Major exchanges and clearinghouses must still cover at least six months of operating costs with qualifying liquid assets.

Still, the change removes a barrier for firms already holding crypto. They can now put some of those assets to work toward regulatory requirements instead of relying entirely on traditional holdings. That could make Bitcoin a little more practical for firms operating inside the US derivatives market.

A move toward $80,000 remains a tall order from here. But Bitcoin and its expanding role in regulated markets are giving us a fresh view to point to, even as the price and chart still need to confirm the recovery.

#5334. So you got a Microsoft Voluntary Exit Offer? Here’s what to do next

by Nikesh Parekh on Nov 19, 2026 at 12:41 pmNovember 19, 2026 at 12:41 pm

Nikesh (Niki) Parekh is a former Microsoft GM who is now CEO of Seattle-based AI talent recruiting startup Provn. This is the fourth post in his series on “Life after Big Tech,” including the Seattle startup guide, laid off at 50 and VC funding is changing dramatically.

Tens of thousands of Microsoft employees have a big decision to make in the next few weeks: take the company’s offer to leave, or stay and take their chances.

Microsoft chief people officer Amy Coleman announced the initiative in a memo on Oct. 26: a Voluntary Exit Offer (VEO) for about 60,000 employees at level 70 and below, which includes general managers and some vice presidents, in the U.S., Canada, the U.K. and India. That’s roughly 27% of Microsoft’s 223,000 people. The company expects 3,000 or fewer of them to accept.

Microsoft says the terms match its standard severance: base pay tied to level and tenure, continued stock vesting, a period of health coverage and career transition help. The severance package varies greatly based on the seniority or level of the employee and the number of years of service. Employees have until early December to decide and would leave by the end of the year.

The offer follows the Voluntary Retirement Program (VRP) that Microsoft extended to about 8,750 U.S. employees in April. About 30% of them, or roughly 2,600 people, took that offer.

All of this comes as Microsoft cuts jobs and changes the kinds of roles it hires for, while pouring money into AI infrastructure and data centers. At the same time, AI is reshaping the broader workforce, flattening management layers and changing what employers look for in new hires.

The worry I hear most is whether more layoffs are waiting on the other side. So the real choice is whether you leave on your own terms or let the company decide for you.

I hear two questions from Microsoft employees thinking about the VEO: How easily can I get another job, and how hard is it to start a company right now?

Harder than you think, and it depends a lot on who you are. We are in the “low hire, low fire” economy.

There is MASSIVE demand for AI-native builders — product managers, data scientists and engineers — as companies adapt products to deal with AI. Companies are also in the process of adopting AI.

One of the fastest-growing tech roles is the “Forward Deployed Engineer,” who implements AI solutions at customers. Security is also job #1 as models and agents get smarter and better at hacking legacy systems.

But it is very hard to be seen by recruiters and hiring managers right now. Candidates are using AI to customize their resumes to each job and using AI agents to apply, sending out 100 to 200 job applications per day. Recruiters are inundated with resumes and job applications, many of which are fake or inappropriate for the role.

It is critical to leverage your network in the job search, which can be hard if you have spent your entire career within one company.

“It has never been easier to build a product, and it has rarely been harder to fund a company.”

Hiring managers have changed what they look for, too. AI fluency is becoming table stakes. The “process” of how you build/sell/market with AI is more important than what you build. Candidates are expected to show prototypes and proof of how they use AI tools every day.

The jobs themselves are changing. A friend told me last month that he wanted an engineering manager role. There are fewer manager roles in the market now.

AI has driven a reduction in management layers and a general flattening of organizations. The engineering team at a small AI company today is a CTO and a group of strong individual contributors. It is normal for managers to have 10 to 30 direct reports now, versus five to 10 in the pre-AI era.

Product management, program management and design teams are shrinking, as well, as AI automates certain jobs.

Hiring managers may view spending your whole career at Microsoft as a yellow flag. Microsoft is an iconic but unusual company. Almost no one else sells to and services customers the way Microsoft does, with an account executive inside nearly every large enterprise in the world.

The skills that get you promoted in Redmond don’t always carry over to a 500- to 5,000-person software company.

It has never been easier to build a product, and it has rarely been harder to fund a company.

Software is cheap to build now. A product leader and an engineer using AI tools can ship in weeks what used to take a team a year.

This cuts both ways for startups. Every good idea attracts a dozen competitors within months, and the big platforms will copy anything that works.

The true strength of a startup today is the ability to grow revenue quickly and establish leadership in a beachhead market. The sales, marketing, product-led growth and distribution strategies are becoming the most critical parts of the business.

The bar for venture funding is extremely high. Jason Lemkin of SaaStr recently shared data from ICONIQ showing that top “AI forward” startups under $10 million in annual recurring revenue are growing 900% a year at the median.

One venture investor told me they advise their portfolio companies that if they aren’t on track for a $10 million run rate within two years, they won’t raise another round. Last week I spoke with an investor who owns part of a business with $4 million in revenue, growing 100% a year and losing $1 million, and it can’t raise.

1) Think VERY big, raise a lot and grow fast enough to justify it. Build an incredible team pursuing an ambitious idea. Raise a large round based on the promise of becoming the next Anthropic, OpenAI or legal AI startup Harvey. Many of the most interesting companies are not software or AI-related, but are “deep tech” companies in defense, robotics, energy and biotech.

2) Raise a moderate amount of money from angels, family offices and nontraditional funds to build a business that has the ability to be profitable on one round of financing. You can control your destiny by building a company that doesn’t rely on the venture capital funding market.

3) Bootstrap and build a business that you own. Fund it yourself, grow it with revenue and get to profitability.

The question that most people are NOT asking is: What do I really want?

Before December, block out an afternoon and think about the last time you were happy at work.

There are many frameworks for figuring out what you want in your career and life in general. I’m a fan of the Four Elements exercise. Write down three times in your career when you felt energized and effective. From those, work out what gives you energy, where you have the most impact, what culture you do best in and what your constraints are: money, kids, aging parents and how many more years you want to work.

On LinkedIn, I have seen examples of Microsoft employees taking the VEO to start their own businesses in property management, buy car washes, take time to recharge, spend time with family and travel.

Other employees are starting the job search in earnest but not taking the VEO. Many others are just getting back to work and doubling down on Microsoft.

Whichever way you go, start now. Start by aligning on your priorities and what you want from your career. If you stay, use the next year to build your skills with AI and to grow a network outside Redmond. If you leave to build something, decide early which of the three funding paths you’re on, because that choice shapes everything that follows.

The people I’ve watched land well after Big Tech had one thing in common: they knew what they wanted before they walked out the door, whether that was a new role, a company of their own or a year with their family.

MediaTek powers more than two billion devices every year, from the most advanced AI infrastructure on the planet to the everyday devices that make life smarter, faster, and more connected. For everyone. MediaTek silicon is the common thread running through all of it. Yeah, MediaTek does that.

#5333. What the year-end board meeting can do for security before the next crisis hits

A high-profile incident can put security at the top of a board’s agenda. Year-end meetings are a chance to keep it there.

This article has been reviewed by the Quartz editorial team. The content may be licensed for reuse.

In November, Nvidia $NVDA opened an independent investigation after reports that its CEO, Jensen Huang, may have been targeted by a foreign intelligence effort. At the time, the company told Reuters that its board had no reason to believe company secrets or U.S. national security had been compromised. The inquiry drew attention to executive security. For other boards, it offers a reason to look back at how security concerns have surfaced at other companies over the year and consider where their own businesses might be exposed.

A fraud case in Hong Kong showed how the apparent involvement of a senior executive can influence an employee’s decision. In 2024, Hong Kong authorities described how an employee approved transfers that cost a company about HK$200 million after a fabricated video meeting appeared to feature its chief financial officer. The case gives directors a concrete issue to consider at year-end. How much authority do employees assume a senior executive has to approve an unusual transaction?

Looking across cases can help directors decide which risks deserve a closer look. A board might review how the company’s public profile changed over the year, then examine which decisions still depend on one executive. It can use that review to decide which procedures staff should test before they have to use them under pressure.

Tim Crockett, co-founder of security advisory firm DGBI-USA, has seen how a crisis exercise can reveal where authority sits in practice. In a crisis exercise he helped run, participants acted on an urgent instruction they believed came from the founder and CEO. The simulation used AI to impersonate the executive, whose reputation for expecting quick action made the request seem plausible. The exercise raises a question for leadership. Would an employee feel comfortable asking for a second check if the request appeared to come from the CEO?

Crockett sees payment approvals as a practical place to start. “A large transfer can require a second sign-off, and several smaller payments may deserve the same scrutiny,” he says. “The same principle applies when an executive makes an exception to the rules for accessing sensitive information. Someone else should review the decision, and there should be a record of it.”

A year-end review can also bring communications, security, and operations teams together. Crockett suggests looking at what the company disclosed through fundraising announcements, executive appearances, and other publicity over the previous year. “Communications staff can identify what became public,” he says. “Security and operations teams can then assess whether those disclosures warrant changes to travel procedures or access to sensitive information. The review can also account for changes abroad.” Crockett sees value in asking how geopolitical developments might affect travel, suppliers, or business continuity in the markets the company relies on.

Before the year-end meeting closes, directors can ask management to identify which lessons from the company’s own experience and from outside incidents apply to the business. Each agreed action should have a person responsible, a deadline, and a way to show whether the change works in practice. Directors can then put those actions on the agenda for the next regular meeting and ask what changed, what an exercise revealed, and which decisions still need their attention.

Crockett says, “Before the next security incident makes headlines, boards should know which safeguards they’ve tested, what those tests revealed, and who’s responsible for closing the gaps.”

#5332. Amazon threatens to leave NYC again, this time over delivery bill, as it rallies customers to fight it

by Kurt Schlosser on Nov 19, 2026 at 12:51 pmNovember 19, 2026 at 12:51 pm

Amazon and New York City are fighting again.

The Seattle tech giant is threatening to move its delivery operations out of the city over a proposed law that would require it to directly employ the drivers who bring packages to New Yorkers’ doors. It’s also asking its customers to help fight the bill.

The legislation, known as the Delivery Protection Act or Intro 518, would apply to companies that run last-mile delivery facilities in the city. Amazon is the main target, but FedEx and several regional couriers would also be covered.

Companies would need a license from the city’s Department of Consumer and Worker Protection, which would also investigate complaints. The bill was introduced in February.

On Thursday, Amazon began showing New York City customers pop-up messages and a homepage banner that reads, “NYC Council could add up to $5 per order. Act now to protect low prices.” The notices link to a form and a pre-written letter customers can send to their council members to oppose the bill, Bloomberg reported. Amazon pointed GeekWire to a study by consulting firm AKRF estimating the bill would raise consumer costs by $409 to $664 a year, but didn’t detail how it arrived at the per-order figure.

In a blog post, Amazon said it relies on a network of small delivery businesses in the city. “If this legislation passes, we’d no longer be able to work with them, and we’d be forced to consider moving our operations outside of the city,” the company wrote. “That would likely mean slower and more expensive delivery for millions of customers in New York City, while also threatening small businesses and their thousands of employees.”

Amazon launched its Delivery Service Partners program in 2018, letting entrepreneurs start their own companies to deliver Amazon packages in Amazon-branded vans and uniforms. The companies hire their own drivers, while Amazon pays them to deliver and offers discounts on vehicles, fuel and insurance. The model lets Amazon expand its delivery network without directly employing drivers.

In a statement to GeekWire, Amazon spokesperson Kelly Nantel said the bill “as written” would threaten more than 40 small delivery businesses the company works with in the city and the more than 5,000 New Yorkers they employ. More than 2,000 Amazon employees also work at its delivery facilities in the city, the company said.

“We’re hopeful this bill doesn’t pass as written,” Nantel said. “But so far, key City Council members seem uninterested in learning about our delivery operations.” Amazon said neither Council Member Tiffany Cabán, the bill’s sponsor, nor Mayor Zohran Mamdani has accepted its offer to visit a delivery facility. The company also said customers sent about 20,000 emails to council members within six hours of the campaign’s launch Thursday morning.

The standoff echoes Amazon’s 2019 reversal on its second headquarters. That February, the company abruptly canceled plans to build a 25,000-person “HQ2” office in Long Island City, Queens, after more than a year of competition among cities to host it. Amazon blamed “a number of state and local politicians” who opposed the project, which drew fierce criticism over roughly $3 billion in government incentives.

Amazon stuck with its plans for Arlington, Va., and Nashville and didn’t reopen its search. Polls at the time showed most New Yorkers supported the deal, but Queens officials, labor leaders and activists fought it. State Sen. Michael Gianaris, who led the opposition, accused Amazon of trying to shake down governments to get its way.

It defies logic that Amazon, a $3 trillion corporation, would raise New Yorkers’ cost of living if it’s forced to adhere to basic regulations and worker protections.We are crafting legislation that regulates Amazon and protects workers, without impacting prices or jobs.If… https://t.co/UWXVTJhRL6

City leaders backing the delivery bill see a familiar pattern. “Amazon is once again making spurious attacks against this commonsense legislation that would make workers and our streets safer,” said Cabán, the bill’s sponsor, who called Amazon’s warning a “dishonest scare tactic.”

City Council Speaker Julie Menin questioned Amazon’s cost claims in a post on X.

“It defies logic that Amazon, a $3 trillion corporation, would raise New Yorkers’ cost of living if it’s forced to adhere to basic regulations and worker protections,” she wrote, adding that the council is “crafting legislation that regulates Amazon and protects workers, without impacting prices or jobs.”

Mamdani endorsed the bill in August, saying Amazon’s subcontractor model “leaves workers vulnerable and corporations free to avoid accountability for reckless conditions on city streets,” CNBC reported.

Supporters, including the Teamsters union, which has sought to organize Amazon drivers and warehouse workers, say the bill would make the work safer and make it harder for Amazon to distance itself from driver injuries.

Amazon disputes that the bill would improve safety. The company said it has invested more than $2.5 billion in driver safety since 2019, that the serious crash rate for its drivers in New York City fell 35.7% from 2024 to 2025, and that drivers there have averaged nearly $24 an hour since January 2025, with required health coverage and paid time off.

Meanwhile, business groups have run ads against the bill and warned they may sue the city if it passes, according to CNBC. The measure is awaiting review by Menin.

#5331. Money habits that show how LeBron James guards small sums and spends big

LeBron James skips data roaming and paid apps, yet his $1.4 billion fortune rests on investing in his body and his businesses.

Most everyday money advice tells people to cut the small charges they pay again and again, such as roaming fees, app subscriptions and premium tiers of services they already use. A person who pays many of them each month can spend a large sum over a year without noticing. That advice is written for households with thin margins, where a few dollars can decide whether a bill gets paid, so it is fair to ask whether it means anything for someone who will never have to worry about money. LeBron James, one of the richest athletes alive, is the sharpest test of that question, because he keeps refusing exactly these charges. He could pay all of them without noticing and still declines. That raises a real question about his fortune: Did the habit help make him rich, or is it simply something he does while being rich?

James has never kept his thrift a secret. He appeared in the 2015 film "Trainwreck," which played his cheapness for laughs, according to CNBC. He chose to make the trait part of his public image, and that makes it read more as a statement of who he is than as a private budgeting system. That matters for how to judge it. A trait someone displays in public can be entirely sincere and still explain very little about where the money came from.

Yahoo Sports set out to show how James's frugal habits fit his status as a billionaire, from listening to Pandora with the commercials to skipping data roaming on trips to Toronto. Those habits are real, and he has kept them for years, so they deserve to be taken seriously as a principle he lives by. The harder question is whether a principle about a few dollars has anything to do with a fortune counted in billions. Answering it means weighing the people who credit his thrift for his wealth against the evidence of where James actually spent his money.

James's teammates noticed his thrift in a daily refusal to pay for something most travelers buy without a second thought. On trips into Canada, he kept his phone off cellular data until he reached Wi-Fi at the team hotel or the arena. He chose to stay offline in a foreign city rather than pay extra to use his phone there. His teammates saw the routine most often in Toronto. Kevin Love, James's former Cavaliers teammate, says he watched it happen there more times than he could count. That repetition turns a skipped charge into a rule. A traveler who forgets to switch on roaming once is careless, but a man who waits for Wi-Fi on every trip has made a decision.

The money at stake was trivial, a roaming fee that former NBA player Tristan Thompson estimated at $40, according to Yahoo Sports. To his teammates, the small size of the charge was the whole point. Love links the habit to an old piece of financial wisdom: losses left unchecked can ruin even the largest fortune, however small each one is. In that view, cutting off minor costs is simply what a careful rich person does. Thompson went further and tied the habit directly to James's wealth. "I guess that's what makes him a billionaire," Thompson said.

LeBron James has claimed his thrift as his own policy, and that puts it on firmer ground than stories told by his teammates. He confirmed the habit himself in a 2017 ESPN interview, Yahoo Sports reports, and he named a short list of small charges he refuses to pay. "No, I'm not doing that. I'm not turning on data roaming, I'm not buying no apps, I still got Pandora with commercials," James said. He could pay for any premium tier and chose the version with ads instead. The refusal is a choice, not a limit on what he can afford.

The rule outlasted the interview by years and carried over to a different platform. In March 2023, James publicly refused to pay for Twitter $TWTR

That is a claim about cause. It comes from people who watched James on the road but never saw his accounts.

The Toronto routine shows how James treats a small charge. Whether that habit explains his fortune is still an open question.

The sums James turns down are too small to matter to someone with his income. His 2023 tweet put the Twitter Blue fee at $5, though the service cost $8 a month at the time, according to CNBC. Next to his Lakers pay of $52,627,153 for the 2025-26 season, either amount is far too small to change his finances in any way. The refusal saves him no money that counts. Its value is symbolic: it shows he will not pay a few dollars he considers wasted.

If the habit cannot explain the fortune, the answer lies in where James has been willing to spend heavily.

James refuses small charges, but he spends freely wherever the money can come back to him. His teammates credit the refused fees for his wealth, yet his fortune, an estimated $1.4 billion according to Forbes figures reported by Yahoo Sports, rests on heavy investment in his body and his businesses. One early deal shows how that kind of investment can pay off. James reportedly took home around $30 million from his share of Beats by Dre when Apple $AAPL bought the company in 2014, according to TIME. That is a different discipline from thrift. It is a rule about where his money goes rather than a rule against spending it.

His spending on his own body, reportedly more than $1 million on health and fitness, looks like a star's indulgence, but it serves the body that earns his salary. James has stretched his career into a 23rd NBA season in 2025-26, according to TIME, and he collects another salary for every year he stays on the court. When James pays for his own upkeep, he is protecting the income his playing career still brings in.

James has made the same choice again and again, taking a share of a business over a one-time payment. With Beats, he took a small equity stake instead of a fee, according to TIME. In 2021 he gave up his small piece of Liverpool in return for a wider stake in Fenway Sports Group, the company that owns the club along with the Red Sox and the Penguins. His holdings also include SpringHill. Set against that pattern, the refused data fees and app upgrades are a real and lasting principle, but they are not where the billions came from.

He guards a few dollars out of conviction, but he got rich by taking a piece of the business.

#5329. GTA VI’s $3.79 billion debut has Zuckerberg joking and Musk laughing, but Take-Two investors still want more

Mark Zuckerberg wanted to know which version of Grand Theft Auto VI he’d bought. On Nov. 20, the Meta CEO posted an edited screenshot on X of one of the game’s in-game prompts: a mission to “pick up groceries” with a pink heart and the line, “Priscilla will appreciate this.” His caption: “Wait which version did I get?”

Elon Musk, the CEO of Tesla and SpaceX, replied with a laughing emoji. The exchange capped the first full day of what is now the biggest entertainment launch on record.

Rockstar Games, the Take-Two Interactive label behind the franchise, said GTA VI generated $3.79 billion in worldwide retail sales on its Nov. 19 release day, based on company estimates. That is more than four times the roughly $800 million GTA V took in on its first day in 2013. The game also sold 32.5 million units before it went on sale.

For scale, the day-one retail figure is more than half of the $6.66 billion in net revenue Take-Two reported for its entire fiscal year ended March 2026. Retail sales account for what consumers spent, not what Take-Two keeps after platform holders and retailers take their cut. Still, the opening validates a bet CEO Strauss Zelnick described to Fortune only as “expensive,” and that one former Take-Two CEO Ben Feder called the last pre-AI blockbuster of its kind.

The sales kept coming after launch day. Research firm Alinea Analytics estimates 44.9 million copies were sold by the end of its opening weekend, grossing more than $4 billion. Take-Two has not confirmed those figures.

Investors were less euphoric. Take-Two shares fell almost 4% on launch day, even as the game earned a 99 on Metacritic. TD Cowen analyst Doug Creutz wrote that the timing and size of the next GTA Online matter more to the stock than GTA VI unit sales.

Take-Two has reiterated its outlook of $8 billion to $8.2 billion in net bookings for fiscal 2027. It has guided to $3.35 billion to $3.5 billion in net bookings for the October–December quarter, the first that will show how much of the launch reaches its books.

Zuckerberg’s joke riffs on a mechanic at the center of GTA VI. Players can build up, or neglect, the relationship between protagonists Jason and Lucia through everyday gestures such as running errands, holding hands, and spending time together. Rockstar North co–studio head Rob Nelson has said the romance is optional, but how players nurture it shapes how the couple’s story unfolds.

That is a departure from the more strictly violence-focused themes of earlier GTA games. Despite complaints from some longtime fans, many players have posted warmly about the pair. Rupert Humphries, Rockstar Games’ senior vice president of narrative, told Game Informer that the realistic domestic dynamic between the Bonnie-and-Clyde-esque leads was meant to immerse players and anchor the story in something positive.

“We wanted to create a world that held up a mirror to that—showed that fever pitch of craziness that we are all maybe a couple of bad decisions away from. But we wanted the story we were going to tell to have something positive at its core and the message that human connection is better than division,” he said.

Emphasizing the couple, rather than violence alone, may also help Rockstar reach players beyond the franchise’s traditionally male-heavy core.

Musk’s reply carried some history. He and Zuckerberg once came close to a cage match. Both later attended President Donald Trump’s second inauguration, and Zuckerberg texted Musk offering to help with his Department of Government Efficiency effort, according to court documents. Some users answered with their own GTA-style notifications, including one with a mission to “fight Elon Musk.”

The post also landed during a rough stretch for tech leaders’ personal lives. Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang resigned on Nov. 12 after admitting to an affair with a woman suspected of being a Chinese spy. Nvidia’s board reinstated him 11 days later, after Trump pressed for his return.

Against that backdrop, and after other tech billionaires, including Jeff Bezos and Bill Gates, faced public reckonings over infidelity, a commenter on his post dubbed him Silicon Valley’s “last wife guy.” It’s an unexpected image for Zuckerberg, who said on Joe Rogan’s podcast in January 2025 that corporate America needed more “masculine energy.”

Zuckerberg met Priscilla Chan, a pediatrician with whom he has three children, in a bathroom line at a Harvard fraternity party. The couple married the day after Facebook went public in 2012.

Since then, Zuckerberg has made grand gestures a habit. He recorded a cover of “Get Low,” the song playing when they met, with T-Pain. He also commissioned a 7-foot statue of Chan and posted it on Instagram with the caption, “bringing back the Roman tradition of making sculptures of your wife.” A grocery run, even a virtual one, is a smaller ask.

#5327. Trump’s Nvidia intervention is the reverse of how Bush handled Enron’s Ken Lay

Once upon a time, a hugely valuable company sat at the cutting edge of an industry the whole economy depended on, and it had close ties to the White House. Then came signs of financial irregularities on a scandalous scale.

That was Enron in 2001, and President George W. Bush stood back and let justice take its course. On Monday, President Donald Trump did the reverse with Nvidia: the chipmaker reinstated Jensen Huang as CEO 11 days after he resigned over reports of extramarital affairs, including one with Alice Huang, a Chinese national U.S. officials suspect of spying and who is no relation.

“I convinced them,” Trump told CNBC in a phone interview. Huang has denied compromising national security, and no one has charged him with a crime.

Nvidia and Enron are not like-for-like scandals, although some commentators see the connection; the details so far are scandalous but are not Enron-style accounting fraud. Still, with some financial commentators fearing an AI bubble could pop and trigger the next financial crisis, Kenneth “Kenny Boy” Lay’s case is instructive. It shows how far Washington has moved from treating big companies as targets to treating them as partners.

Lay was a fixture of Houston’s energy establishment, and his ties to the Bush family went back to the first President Bush. Bush adviser Karl Rove later called any idea that Lay was a “close intimate” of Bush “ludicrous,” but they were close enough that Bush gave him the “Kenny Boy” nickname.

The money was never in doubt. Across Bush’s political career, Enron, its employees and their families gave him more than $550,000, more than any other single source, and Lay was his biggest financial backer.

As Texas governor, Bush signed a 1999 electricity deregulation law that opened new markets to Enron. During the 2000 campaign, he traveled to Houston for the Astros’ first game at Enron Field, where Lay threw out the first pitch.

Wall Street loved the company, too. Fortune named Enron America’s most innovative company six years running, even as Fortune’s Bethany McLean became the first major business journalist to ask, in March 2001, how exactly Enron made its money.

When Enron was collapsing in October 2001, Lay phoned Treasury Secretary Paul O’Neill and Commerce Secretary Donald Evans. Both said they did nothing to help. Nearly five years later, with Bush still in the White House, a jury convicted Lay and former CEO Jeffrey Skilling of fraud.

Skilling’s 24-year sentence was among the longest ever handed to a corporate executive; a judge cut it to 14 years in 2013. Former CFO Andrew Fastow got six years and was released after about five. Lay died before he could be sentenced, and his convictions were vacated.

The two companies already share a footnote. At the end of November 2001, days before Enron filed for bankruptcy, Standard & Poor’s dropped it from the S&P 500 and replaced it with a Santa Clara graphics-chip maker called Nvidia.

Huang’s closeness to Trump is newer, and he built it deliberately. CNBC reports that Huang spent two years cultivating an “unparalleled relationship” with Trump while Nvidia lobbied for looser limits on selling advanced chips to China.

Nvidia gave $1 million to Trump’s inaugural fund and $25 million to his White House ballroom, and it initially sought to keep the ballroom gift anonymous. In April 2025, Huang attended a $1-million-a-head dinner at Mar-a-Lago, after which the administration briefly held off on restricting Nvidia’s H20 chips before imposing the limits days later.

By July, the administration had reversed course and begun approving sales to China, and in December Trump said Nvidia could sell its more powerful H200 chips to approved Chinese customers. Democrats, including Sen. Chris Van Hollen of Maryland, have tied the donations to those decisions, but there is no known hard evidence of any specific quid pro quo — something that could change under the incoming, heavily Democratic Congress.

Nvidia shares closed up about 31.5% on Monday, their best day since 2003, adding $952 billion in market value, and the S&P 500 rose 4.73%. The rebound reversed much of the slide that followed Huang’s exit, although the stock gave back single-digit percentages on Tuesday and Wednesday.

The stakes are hard to overstate. Nvidia ranks No. 16 on the 2026 Fortune 500 and was the first company on the list to top $4 trillion in market value.

Trump held between $13 million and $58 million in Nvidia stock at the end of 2025, according to his Office of Government Ethics filings, and CBS News estimated his stake gained between $1.3 million and $14.8 million on Monday. The White House told CBS that independent managers run his portfolio.

Nvidia matters well beyond the president’s portfolio. The company, and Huang personally, have been called “the central bank of AI,” a label The Economist applied after tallying more than $70 billion in Nvidia investments in startups over three years and $300 billion in financial support to customers.

Owen Lamont, a portfolio manager at Acadian Asset Management who writes the Owenomics newsletter, says that label carries a curse. In his telling, once an entity is called “the central bank of” its field, it becomes “a prime candidate for a cosmic smackdown.”

Long-Term Capital Management, called “the central bank of volatility” before its 1998 collapse, was the first victim he knows of. FTX, called “the central bank of crypto” six months before Sam Bankman-Fried’s arrest, was the second.

The Economist has also compared Nvidia’s financing to the vendor lending Cisco and Lucent did in the dot-com boom. Cisco is the other fallen high-flier Nvidia is most often measured against, usually by outlier voices; it is the favorite comparison of “Big Short” trader Michael Burry, who has become a Substack star during the AI boom.

The Enron prosecutions marked the end of an era. In “The Chickenshit Club,” ProPublica’s Jesse Eisinger holds up a Justice Department that set up a dedicated task force, charged nearly all of Enron’s top executives and did so against a friend of the president. He argues that the department has since lost the will and ability to prosecute top executives.

The title comes from James Comey, who led the FBI’s 2016 investigation of Hillary Clinton’s emails and is now fighting a third attempt by Trump’s Justice Department to prosecute him. As U.S. attorney in Manhattan, Comey told prosecutors who had never lost a trial that they belonged to the “Chickenshit Club,” meaning they were too cautious to take on hard cases.

After the financial crisis, a University of Chicago Law Review article noted that Kareem Serageldin, a Credit Suisse banker sentenced to 30 months, was the only banker jailed in the U.S. for a role in the crash. In 2013, Attorney General Eric Holder told the Senate that the size of some banks had “an inhibiting impact” on prosecutions; he later said banks were not too big to jail.

In Eisinger’s telling, that retreat left prosecutors unwilling to pursue big-company executives. Trump has now gone further, treating companies less as targets than as partners.

He has used the pardon power liberally in both terms. He pardoned Nikola founder Trevor Milton, who had been sentenced to four years for securities and wire fraud, and Binance founder Changpeng Zhao in October 2025. A not-yet-published study reported by Law360 found that 49 of Trump’s 89 pardons unrelated to Jan. 6 or the fake-elector scheme went to white-collar defendants.

His administration has also taken a 10% stake in Intel, a golden share in U.S. Steel and a 15% cut of Nvidia and AMD chip sales to China. Foreign Policy describes it as state capitalism of a kind few predecessors embraced.

Nvidia now sits in that company. A person familiar with the matter told CNBC that Trump and Vice President JD Vance were briefed and saw no evidence Huang did anything illegal. Attorney General Todd Blanche publicly called Nvidia “a good corporate citizen” but declined to say whether investigators had examined Huang.

Other probes continue. The Securities and Exchange Commission is conducting a civil investigation of Nvidia, The Wall Street Journal has reported, and California Attorney General Rob Bonta has subpoenaed the company.

Whether this becomes a political scandal is unsettled. AI skeptic Gary Marcus asked in his Substack newsletter this week whether “Jensengate” could take down the president, writing that “you can bet your last dollar the incoming Congress is going to take an interest.”

When Enron collapsed, Lay called two members of Bush’s Cabinet, and both said they did nothing to help. When Nvidia’s chief executive was ousted, Trump openly said he brokered the deal to bring him back.

“I didn’t use the word ‘prosecuted,’” Trump told CNBC. “I said that we believe he’s fine. He’s absolutely fine. I gave them enough assurance.”

The next test comes Dec. 3, when Huang is scheduled to appear at a public Senate Banking Committee hearing. The Enron precedent suggests why lawmakers may keep pressing: it took years and a dedicated task force for Bush’s Justice Department to finish.

Nick Lichtenberg is business editor and was formerly Fortune's executive editor of global news.

#5325. StepSecurity, led by two Microsoft vets, raises $20M to defend developers’ tools from hackers

Chronicling the Seattle and Pacific Northwest startup scene. SEE MORE

by Todd Bishop on Nov 20, 2026 at 8:28 amNovember 20, 2026 at 8:34 am

StepSecurity’s co-founders spent more than two decades combined at Microsoft. This week, as their startup announced a new round of funding, its researchers were also investigating a hacked Microsoft software package.

Their old employer is not the only one with this problem.

StepSecurity, a Seattle-area cybersecurity startup, raised a $20 million Series A round led by Elephant, with participation from existing investors Runtime Ventures, Inner Loop Capital and SaaS Ventures. The company has now raised $23 million, including a $3 million seed round in 2024. Axios Pro first reported the latest round.

The startup protects the systems used to build software: developers’ laptops, code repositories, package downloads and CI/CD pipelines, the automated systems that assemble and ship code.

The problem is that attackers increasingly slip malicious code into open-source software that developers download. That code can do damage as soon as it runs on a developer’s laptop or build system, stealing the passwords and keys that unlock other systems.

“A supply chain attack used to take a skilled team,” CEO Varun Sharma wrote in a blog post announcing the funding. “Now one person can vibe code it.”

Sharma spent about 15 years at Microsoft, where he led a team in Azure Security focused on making security easier for developers. CTO Ashish Kurmi spent nearly eight years at Microsoft before leading cloud security at Uber and infrastructure security at Plaid.

The two met at Microsoft and started StepSecurity in 2021, after working through the fallout from the SolarWinds and Codecov supply chain attacks at their respective employers.

A busy week: The Microsoft package, agent-framework, is the Python version of Microsoft’s open-source toolkit for building AI agents.

It gets roughly 190,000 downloads a month. Two malicious versions published on Nov. 17 to PyPI, the main public repository for Python software, included code designed to steal cloud and CI/CD credentials as soon as Python started up, SecurityWeek reported. PyPI quarantined both versions, and a Microsoft maintainer said an investigation was underway.

That’s one entry in a long list. StepSecurity’s announcement also cites the $6.3 billion Binance breach in October, which the FBI attributed to North Korea’s TraderTraitor group. Binance has said the attack started with a compromised employee laptop.

It also points to a tampered copy of Anthropic’s Claude Code extension that sat in Cursor’s extension marketplace for about 11 hours last month. Cursor said up to 5,000 users may have received the malicious version.

StepSecurity says it documented 56 confirmed compromises of trusted software components between August 2025 and August 2026, and roughly one every three days from March 2026 through the August report.

How it works: StepSecurity got its start with its own tool, Harden-Runner, which is free for open-source projects. It watches automated builds on GitHub and flags anything unexpected in the processes they run, the network connections they make or the files they change.

More than 20,000 open-source projects use it, the company says, up from about 3,000 at the time of the seed round. Unusual behavior spotted in those public builds has helped StepSecurity catch attacks early, the company says, including the March 2025 compromise of tj-actions, a widely used add-on for GitHub’s build automation.

StepSecurity’s paid products also protect developers’ laptops and check code repositories. Its Secure Registry service screens software packages before a company’s builds download them from public sources such as npm, the main public repository for JavaScript packages. It blocks versions known to be compromised and holds brand-new releases for a waiting period, giving researchers time to catch malicious ones before anyone installs them.

Along with the funding, StepSecurity is making Secure Registry free for public GitHub projects that use Harden-Runner and run their builds on GitHub’s servers. The free version defaults to a two-day waiting period and supports JavaScript packages, with Python, Java, Ruby and Rust planned.

StepSecurity has plenty of competition. Socket, a San Francisco startup that screens open-source packages for malicious code, raised $60 million at a $1 billion valuation in May. Sonatype, JFrog and Endor Labs also sell tools that can block risky packages before they’re installed.

Growth spurt: StepSecurity says its annual recurring revenue grew fivefold in 2024, fivefold again in 2025 and more than fivefold so far this year. It didn’t disclose dollar figures.

Named customers include Circle, Dexcom, Kong, Mercari, Chainguard and XBOW.

The company has 27 employees, up from four, including the founders, at the time of the seed round. Sharma is based in Sammamish and Kurmi in Kirkland, and the rest of the remote-first team is spread across the U.S., Canada and India.

What’s next: StepSecurity plans to extend its protections to agent sandboxes, the isolated environments where AI agents run code. Its argument is that anyone who asks an AI agent for a spreadsheet may be downloading and running open-source packages.

The company says it also plans to double its team over the next 12 months, mostly in security research, engineering and sales and marketing.

#5324. The FCC gave SpaceX approval for up to 1 million AI data centers in space

The approval is granted in part with conditions, and SpaceX must file more orbital debris plans before deploying satellites above 600 km

The Federal Communications Commission authorized SpaceX to deploy up to 1 million satellites that would operate as data centers in space, according to an order the agency released on Wednesday.

The FCC's Space Bureau granted SpaceX's application in part and deferred part of it, with conditions. The authority covers radio communications for the constellation, called Starmind, that serve as a fallback and in emergencies to carry telemetry and to track and command the satellites, in the 18.8-19.3 GHz and 28.6-29.1 GHz bands. SpaceX must operate in those bands on an unprotected, non-interference basis. The satellites will rely on optical links for their primary communications, the order said.

The constellation would sit in orbital shells at altitudes from 500 to 1,002 kilometers (311 to 623 miles). The FCC deferred SpaceX's request for a waiver of the rule requiring satellites that end their missions below 2,000 kilometers (1,243 miles) to be disposed of through atmospheric re-entry. Before deploying any satellites that operate above 600 kilometers (373 miles), SpaceX must file an application to modify the authorization with a final orbital debris mitigation plan.

The grant sets deployment milestones. SpaceX must deploy one satellite by Nov. 25, 2033, 10% of the authorized satellites by Nov. 25, 2035, and 50% by Nov. 25, 2038. It must launch the remainder by Nov. 25, 2040, or the authorization becomes null and void. The license term is 15 years and begins when SpaceX certifies that the first Starmind satellite is in orbit and operating under the authorization's terms.

Three parties filed petitions to deny the application: Kuiper Systems, which operates as Amazon $AMZN Leo; Viasat; and the American Astronomical Society. The bureau said it dismissed environmental and optical astronomy concerns as matters outside the Commission's authority.

The proposal prompted a comment tally from the public north of 1,500, according to Bloomberg. FCC Chairman Brendan Carr said the commission was, for the first time, approving orbital data centers.

SpaceX had revealed the design of its first orbital data center satellite, called AI1, in a video posted to X $TWTR in June, ahead of its IPO. The orbital compute initiative was central to the company's pitch to investors.

The FCC is weighing other proposals for data centers in orbit and plans to rule on every one, according to The Wall Street Journal. Blue Origin has also applied to the FCC to put its own data centers into orbit and is still waiting for a decision, according to Bloomberg.

#5322. Walmart’s shopper base is shifting: High earners lead its gains as low-income shoppers turn to Amazon

Walmart is known for its bargains, but its growth increasingly comes from shoppers who don’t strictly need them. Six-figure households like a good deal, too.

Upper-income households led Walmart’s U.S. market-share gains, the company said Nov. 19 as it reported fiscal third-quarter results. Revenue rose 5.2% to $188.8 billion from $179.5 billion a year earlier and topped Wall Street’s forecasts for both sales and profit.

E-commerce did the heavy lifting. U.S. online sales rose 23%, the 11th straight quarter up more than 20%, while global e-commerce grew 17%.

“We delivered strong results, growing our core business and gaining market share,” CEO John Furner said in the release. Walmart raised its full-year outlook for the third time this year and now expects net sales growth of 4.9% to 5.2% and adjusted earnings per share of $2.84 to $2.89, up from $2.80 to $2.87.

Not everything accelerated. U.S. comparable sales rose 2.9%, well below the 4.5% gain a year earlier, and the new outlook came in more conservative than analysts expected, the Associated Press reported.

The split matters well beyond Bentonville. With more than 150 million customers shopping its stores or website each week, Walmart is one of the clearest windows into American spending heading into the holidays, and right now that window shows higher earners stepping up while others pull back.

Furner said in February that most of Walmart’s share gains came from households earning more than $100,000, and in June he told reporters that higher-income customers were visiting more often and buying more.

The new customers also skew young. At Sam’s Club, Gen Z and millennials made up more than half of new sign-ups in the quarter, and more than half of that group chose the pricier Plus tier.

Convenience is a big part of the pitch. Mobile ordering, free pickup, and fast delivery let customers fill a grocery cart, pick up prescriptions, and stock the garden in one stop, and Walmart said its biggest market-share gains in three years came in food, CNBC reported.

Membership is the next lever. In October, Walmart launched a $120-a-year bundle of Walmart+ and Sam’s Club Plus, nearly $100 less than buying both separately.

“It does help at a time when we do see some customers showing some signs of pressure,” Furner told Fox News Digital at the launch, pointing to higher energy costs.

Walmart’s stores power its online business. The company said more than 80% of U.S. e-commerce orders, including third-party marketplace orders, are fulfilled from stores, letting it deliver a wide assortment faster.

Fuel costs have tested that network this year. Diesel hit a record national average of $6.53 a gallon on Sept. 22, according to AAA, a surge CBS News reported was especially painful for farmers and small businesses.

Prices have since eased, with diesel falling below $6 in mid-November for the first time in two months as President Trump signaled he wouldn’t escalate the war in Iran. Furner told CNBC the retailer aims to keep prices low despite fuel costs, and Walmart ended the quarter with about 7,700 rollbacks.

Advertising is padding the margins. Walmart U.S. ad sales rose 37% in the quarter, and WARC platform benchmarks put Walmart’s average return on ad spend about 25% above Amazon’s.

Walmart’s global ad business brought in roughly $6.4 billion last fiscal year, per WARC. That’s far behind Amazon’s roughly $68 billion but well ahead of Target’s Roundel and of Instacart and DoorDash combined.

Not every customer is on board. Numerator data released days before the earnings report showed Walmart stores lost 5.6% of their low-income purchasing households, and the ones who stayed made fewer trips.

Among low-income shoppers cutting back on Walmart store visits, 51% named Amazon as an alternative, ahead of local grocery stores and dollar stores.

That rivalry has already cost Walmart a crown. Amazon ended Walmart’s 13-year run atop the Fortune 500 this year, and Walmart now ranks No. 2 on the 2026 Fortune 500, with $713.2 billion in revenue.

Furner’s answer is to pull every part of the business into the fight. “From membership and agentic shopping to new ways of using our stores and delivery network, we’re bringing the best of Walmart together to serve customers better and create new opportunities for growth,” he said.

#5321. How the surge in AI-discovered bugs is straining Microsoft security and threatening tech stability

by Angela Gunn on Nov 20, 2026 at 9:25 amNovember 20, 2026 at 9:25 am

It has come to the attention of the general public this month that adversaries successfully adopt technology a lot faster than defenders do. This has nothing to do with the willingness of defenders to try. It has everything to do with the ancient truth that to succeed, defenders have to get it right every time but adversaries only have to get it right occasionally.

Now multiply “every time” and “occasionally” by AI. Do you like that math? Does anyone?

The disastrous update that broke Teams, Outlook, SharePoint and other packages was not a direct attack by AI-wielding bad guys. Nor was the FAA outage. Nor were most of the outage events of the past few weeks, though who can say what’s up with those European Union refrigerators.

No. The true AI-driven mayhem has been predicated for several months now not on powerful new AI-honed attacks, but on an absolute deluge of bugs of relatively low severity that Microsoft and other defenders with a formal patch process aren’t built to process.

The question is whether traditional patch programs can adapt their processes to handle the deluge. Microsoft’s is MAPP (Microsoft Active Protections Program), to which the company has been committed for nearly two decades. If the industry-spanning events of the past few weeks are any indication, these programs can’t.

Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella said Wednesday at the New York Times DealBook Summit that last week’s Microsoft 365 outage came from a latent bug and wasn’t directly tied to AI, but he warned that AI-driven patching could bring more instability.

He elaborated in a separate appearance on CNBC the same day, saying the flood of patches being applied to older infrastructure is making systems less stable.

AI has “allowed us to find these bugs and fix these bugs, but that means you’ve got to then patch them, and that creates instability,” Nadella said, when asked by Jim Cramer about a string of recent outages at United, Schwab, Chase and other organizations.

Some context: MAPP turned 18 this year. The program, run by the MSRC (Microsoft Security Response Center), handles outreach to partner companies that gain early access to information on the bugs in advance of each month’s Patch Tuesday release. In-house, it coordinates the patch release process, just as the larger MSRC organization helps coordinate the handling of bug reports from external finders.

MSRC also runs point on prioritizing patches of the worst bugs through its SSIRP (Software and Services Incident Response Plan) program, itself dating to 2004. In its time, it was an industry leader in how companies can efficiently get their arms around bad bugs.

MAPP in its own way is similarly remarkable. It has undergone a few traumas over the years, usually when a partner breaks confidence and leaks the advance details it receives. In 2025, after attacks on SharePoint raised suspicions of a leak from the program, Microsoft stopped giving Chinese companies early access. But MAPP continues to tick along in a way that would make any program manager proud. Other companies have their own version of MAPP / MSRC, as do community efforts such as those supporting Linux.

Full disclosure: I’m a former MSRC employee who learned about MAPP at the knee of the program’s principals. I subsequently tracked patch releases at a company partnered with MAPP at its highest (Validate) level, which means I was privy to the 14-day multi-stage run-up to each month’s release. I admire and respect the program… and I’m afraid that in the AI-finder era, it’s in big, big trouble.

Since January 2021, Microsoft has issued patches for an estimated 10,319 CVEs. (I use estimated numbers throughout this analysis because there are various ways of counting such things, including whether or not the patch accrues to an application such as Edge, which actually relies on the Chromium project for its fixes. Other analysts arrive at larger or smaller counts.)

Over half of those — 5,383 CVEs — are 2026 releases, 5,128 of which were addressed since April. In comparison, 2025’s full-year CVE total was 1,180.

What happened in April? As nearly as analysis can determine, the floodgates opened and finders (security researchers) started barraging the company with reports.

The first quarter of 2026 saw 255 CVEs addressed over three months. April had 163, May 132; in June the number jumped to 209. In July it was off to the races with 575 CVEs. In October, the monthly count topped 1,400.

Most of these bugs aren’t coming from the usual security stalwarts. They’re coming from new finders, they’re coming in with multiple simultaneous finders not believed to be working together, and they’re coming in relatively weak.

Though the overall volume has skyrocketed, the number per month of bugs under active exploit in the wild — the notorious “zero-days” — hasn’t increased proportionally.

Moreover, average bug severity has in fact decreased. Until 2026, the average CVSS severity score for all bugs tended to hover around 7.8 (out of 10) each month. In 2026, that’s dropped to approximately 7.4 as of September — not garbage finds, but the sort of thing that doesn’t scramble the jets.

No surge in zero-days and a drop in severity — that’s good news. The problem is the volume.

Once bugs are received by Microsoft, each goes through a MAPP-helmed, multi-team process of investigation and patch development.

The true AI-driven mayhem has been predicated not on powerful new AI-honed attacks, but on a deluge of bugs of relatively low severity that Microsoft and others aren’t built to process.

Since many products have several versions still in support, that often means that multiple teams within each product group are asked to ingest a bug report, replicate the problem, devise and test a fix, ensure the fix doesn’t trigger other problems or inadvertently point to a similar bug elsewhere in the product and ready it for mass consumption. Even AI slop has to be taken seriously, just in case.

Meanwhile, MAPP is the traffic cop for the entire release, working with each team to ascertain patches are ready, understand the nature of the bugs and what can be safely communicated to partners and the public, and ready the processes that make the second Tuesday of each month a festival of downloads and reboots. From where we stand right now, it’s all fairly… hand-crafted.

In theory the process is automatable to some extent, though the success of that effort so far in light of recent events is debatable. But high volume also leads to other problems, such as exposing information on incomplete patching.

For instance, Microsoft has recently patched Office bugs that apply to both Windows and Mac, but patches have initially only been available for Windows versions.

Microsoft’s release-day information about such bugs — patching Windows versions while asking Apple users to monitor Microsoft communications for news of their own patch — alerts the world, including eager adversaries, that the flaw exists. Apple customers just have to hope no adversaries exploit it while their patch is pending.

More broadly, many of the steps in the current patching process involve judgment calls, not processes that scale well or that can reliably be handled by existing AI-driven systems. In Microsoft’s case, MAPP is a remarkably small team of humans and, being security folk at Microsoft, they’re not always the loudest or most popular voice in Redmond.

Add the mercurial nature of finders, who may or may not provide full details on their bugs (ask any MSRC person how often they receive a crash dump and a demand for payment) and may or may not disclose their finds publicly if they don’t feel they’re getting sufficient response.

Do not add the kind of defender staffing needed to handle a massive increase in volume — either in MAPP or in the individual product groups building the actual patches — because in the AI era, it’s likely the companies won’t add it either.

The cracks are showing. Microsoft has been compelled to issue OOB (out-of-band) releases and servicing updates monthly since July, often within just a few days of the original release.

OOBs are important enough to merit release outside the usual patch cadence, often because there’s a security issue involved, but they’re tough on administrators already wading through a slew of regularly scheduled patching. With volumes high, patch testers may rush or elide certain steps, such as checking that a fix doesn’t break something deeper in the system.

Nadella told the DealBook audience this week that a patch for a critical bank system might once have been tested for a week. Now, he said, the patch “needs to go instantly from being available to being patched in production because it’s being exploited in the wild. So that’s going to create instability.”

Think of MAPP as Mariners catcher Dan Wilson in 2001: a pro handling a staff of skilled human pitchers, one pitch at a time. Now it’s 2026, and the pitchers have been swapped for a bank of mediocre pitching machines all slinging fastballs at … 2026-era Dan Wilson.

Here, again, AI can’t fix a system that requires defenders to catch every pitch. Secondary lines of defense that have worked in the past — for instance, the requirement by various regulatory programs that enterprises ascertain that patches are safe for their own systems — rely heavily on companies sending out the soundest possible patches.

Managed service providers might at least make sure that patches are flagged to customers as available, relevant and urgent. But they’re in no position to do much more than trust that what’s shipped is safe to deploy and react when things go wrong.

Even that gets harder when a bug kneecaps the security tools they depend on. Last week’s Microsoft 365 outage affected parts of Microsoft Defender that interact with Exchange Online.

It’s not just Microsoft, of course. The Linux community is seriously suffering, and both Apple and (especially) Google have struggled with patch-release quality in 2026 as evidenced by their own emergency updates and post-release device instability reports. Industry-wide, ecosystems built around reliable, transparent patch cadences and patch-development processes have never seemed more in danger of being overwhelmed.

What needs to happen? Sure, build those AI systems; the marketing people will be pleased. It’ll speed up some parts of the process. But a system capable of replicating, every time, the human judgment calls that go into the patch-release process isn’t going to magically create itself; people have to create it.

Is there some chance that the deluge will ebb — that researchers and their tools will at some point finally find all the bugs in all the world’s products?

It’s a pretty thought, and some relief may eventually come. When more and more unrelated finders turn up the same bug, it gives one hope that the set is finite. But no one knows when relief will come, and most folk in tech suspect that really, no, there is no bottom to the bug barrel. Nor, for the foreseeable future, any rest for the weary.

MediaTek powers more than two billion devices every year, from the most advanced AI infrastructure on the planet to the everyday devices that make life smarter, faster, and more connected. For everyone. MediaTek silicon is the common thread running through all of it. Yeah, MediaTek does that.
