#5304. Thinking About a Second Location? Here Are 5 Signs You’re Ready

You're viewing the US website. Looking for the Site edition?

Before you open a second location, take a hard look at what makes the first one work.

Opinions expressed by Entrepreneur contributors are their own.

A thriving first business location can make opening another feel like the obvious next move. But before you open a second, take a hard look at what makes the first one work. Can your team repeat that success while you divide your time between two businesses?

I judge business success partly by whether the business is growing. That doesn’t mean chasing every opportunity or signing a lease just because a space becomes available. Growth should be calculated, with the people, money, and commitment to support it.

Franchise owners already have a business model to follow, but they still have to build a strong operation in each market. Here are five signs I look for in deciding whether to expand, plus one that overrides them all.

Start with an honest look at your financials. Strong sales are encouraging, but steady profitability tells you more about whether your business is ready to expand.

Look beyond a great month or a busy season. Your first location should generate enough to cover operating expenses, royalties, financing obligations, and a reasonable salary for you, with money left over. Review both profitability and cash flow, since they don’t always move together.

Also, consider how the business performs during slower periods. If it needs constant cash infusions to get through normal seasonal fluctuations, strengthening that operation should come first.

Next, separate the cost of opening from the cost of getting established. You’ll need money for both.

A new location may take time to attract customers and cover its expenses. Therefore, your budget should account for startup costs, ongoing operating needs, and a cushion for delays or slower sales. Build that plan around realistic assumptions about your brand and market.

Before adding another unit, ask yourself what happens if it takes longer than expected to gain traction. You should be able to support the launch while protecting the original business’s working capital. Otherwise, one difficult opening could put both operations under pressure.

Can you leave for a week without the operation falling apart? That’s a useful test because a second business will (or should) demand a great deal of your attention.

Some of our franchise owners have told me, “Man, I left for a week, and we had our best week ever.” Once you get over the discovery that you’re not irreplaceable, take that as an encouraging sign.

However, you need more than one dependable person. Look for employees who can step into leadership roles, supported by clear expectations, training, and regular reporting.

Our company has a policy of promoting leaders from within. Existing team members already know your standards and your customers. They’ll still need management training, but you’re building on an established relationship. If you hire externally, give yourself enough time to bring that person into the business before opening day.

Pay attention to where your customers live and work. A steady stream from a nearby area may suggest an opportunity to serve them closer to home.

It doesn’t prove there’s no competition, though. Nor does it guarantee enough demand to support another unit. Instead, treat those customers as a starting point for research.

Study the area’s demographics, competitors, site access and territory availability with your franchisor. Then consider whether the new business will attract additional customers or mainly shift sales away from your first location.

You want evidence that the opportunity extends beyond a handful of enthusiastic requests to open closer to someone’s neighborhood.

Financial readiness matters, but so do your expectations. You need the patience to let a new operation establish itself.

When I started Signarama 40 years ago, people compared it with Minuteman Press, which my dad had founded. Minuteman had been operating for 20 years. Yet people still pointed to its higher earnings as evidence that it was the better business.

That wasn’t a useful comparison. One business had a long history; the other was just getting started.

Similarly, when you open a second location, measure it against realistic launch milestones. Track its progress in sales, customer retention, and operating performance. Use what you learned in the original business, while recognizing that the new team needs time to build relationships and momentum.

Finally, you have to care enough to show up and do the work.

I recently spoke with a franchise owner who had opened another location in a different state. He hadn’t visited in 90 days. He said things were going fine, but I told him he needed to be there regularly, especially during the startup period.

If you want to grow, you have to go. That’s it. You don’t have a choice. You have to be there on a consistent basis. I go to Australia every year to visit with our franchisees there, and I was in India recently for grand openings of two new locations for one of our brands.

All the signs about financing and staffing and market penetration mean nothing if you don’t care about doing everything you can to make your new location a success. Are you committed to the expansion?

If you’re not committed to it, fully committed to it, don’t do it.

A thriving first business location can make opening another feel like the obvious next move. But before you open a second, take a hard look at what makes the first one work. Can your team repeat that success while you divide your time between two businesses?

I judge business success partly by whether the business is growing. That doesn’t mean chasing every opportunity or signing a lease just because a space becomes available. Growth should be calculated, with the people, money, and commitment to support it.

Franchise owners already have a business model to follow, but they still have to build a strong operation in each market. Here are five signs I look for in deciding whether to expand, plus one that overrides them all.

#5303. GTA VI was built by hand. The man who ran Take-Two during GTA IV says AI could let a filmmaker make the next breakout game

Grand Theft Auto VI, on track to be the biggest entertainment launch of any kind, was made the old-fashioned way: Take-Two Interactive CEO Strauss Zelnick said in February that Rockstar Games built the game without generative AI.

“With regards to GTA 6, generative AI has zero part in what Rockstar Games is building. Their worlds are handcrafted. That’s what differentiates them,” Zelnick told GamesIndustry.biz. “They’re built from the ground up, building by building, street by street, neighborhood by neighborhood.”

That’s not to say it didn’t take time and money. Analysts estimate Take-Two spent more than a billion dollars on the game, which came out more than 13 years after its predecessor (Take-Two CEO Strauss Zelnick never confirmed the amount but admitted the game was “expensive”). But the next blockbuster video game might come sooner, cheaper—and with an even more cinematic lens, according to Ben Feder, who ran Take-Two Interactive when Grand Theft Auto IV came out in 2008.

“Some great creative mind who would have otherwise gone to make a film will make a video game because it’s as simple as point and click,” Feder said to Fortune in a long-winding conversation that quickly became more philosophical than experiential about the state of the entertainment industry.

Feder, now managing partner of TIRTA Ventures, said in a Fortune commentary this month that AI will change how big games get made. His firm invests in AI-native game projects. “We put our money where our mouth is,” he said of TIRTA’s investments.

The next great video game maker might be someone who would otherwise have gone into movies, and that’s because AI would make it easier for a filmmaker without a technical background to get into video games. And Feder doesn’t expect that shift to hurt the franchise he once oversaw.

“I don’t think GTA is going anywhere. In fact, it probably goes from strength to strength,” Feder said. “But that’s not to say it’s going to get created in the exact same way that it got created here.”

Video games have long sat at the intersection of the software and entertainment businesses. Feder said AI will shrink the software side as writing code gets cheaper and easier.

“The argument would be that because AI is making software development commoditized, and software points to zero, it becomes much more about entertainment than it does about both entertainment and computer science,” he said.

Feder described the result as “somewhere between democratizing creativity, the cynic would say commoditizing creativity, but I don’t believe that creativity, true creativity, really gets commoditized unless you’re such a believer in AI that you think AI can also be creative.”

More games won’t mean more hits. Feder expects a flood of new titles, with only a small share breaking through, and pointed to YouTube.

“I don’t know how many billions of minutes of video have been on YouTube, but how many of them actually are good? How many of them actually get traction?” he said. “But the ones that do get traction and are good reach billions of people, literally, and can create enormous outcomes, both creatively and commercially.”

Grand Theft Auto VI shows how large those outcomes can be. Take-Two has not disclosed the game’s cost, though estimates put its development budget at $1 billion to $1.5 billion. Brokerage Oppenheimer projected about $1.85 billion in gross revenue in the game’s first three days, Reuters reported.

“Thirteen years of investment you make back in a day. Unbelievable,” Feder said. “But it only happens if you create the most awesome game ever.”

AI tools could change that math across the industry, he said. “It’s going to get harder to justify a $2 billion game in a world where the next best alternative is two orders of magnitude less.”

GTA VI, ironically, did make back all the money it poured into it, and then some. Feder said that counterargument is a pretty good devil’s advocate. “What’s the argument for not spending another $2 billion on the next one and making it back in a day?” he said. “That’s a valid argument.”

At this point, the conversation became a lived experience of the entertainment industry at large. While most people think of film and cinema as making up the lion’s share of what people consider entertainment, video games have always been there, and they’ve been blockbusters of their own. But recently, as with movies, it seems big publishers have long concentrated their money on a handful of games, or, as the Marvel Cinematic Universe has shown, on the franchise model.

“Even when I was at Take-Two for GTA IV, we were the first, and others followed, to develop a strategy of fewer, bigger titles,” Feder said. And just like movies, the non-Indie games have a tough time breaking through the noise. Feder said the pressure falls on games in the middle, those with big budgets and smaller audiences.

Feder said that when he ran Take-Two, he saw the industry’s next frontier as characters that look like movie actors rather than figures in a game. Of GTA VI, he said, “This gets as close to it as I’ve ever seen.”

Catherina covers markets, the economy, energy, tech, and AI.

#5301. An Email Avalanche Is Coming to Your Customers on Black Friday. Here’s How to Make Sure Yours Reaches Them

You're viewing the US website. Looking for the Site edition?

Black Friday inboxes are brutally crowded. Here’s how to avoid the deliverability mistakes that can send your campaign to spam before customers ever see your offer.

Opinions expressed by Entrepreneur contributors are their own.

Black Friday is one of the few days of the year when customers expect companies to flood their inboxes. And flood them they do.

In 2025, brands using Mailchimp sent 1.39 billion emails on Black Friday alone. Cyber Monday brought another 1.3 billion. For founders preparing holiday campaigns, that volume creates a problem that has little to do with whether your subject line is clever or your discount is generous.

Your emails have to reach the inbox first.

During Cyber Week, many companies increase their sending volume, sometimes overnight. At the same time, Gmail, Yahoo, Microsoft and other inbox providers are evaluating whether senders deserve access to the inbox. That makes Black Friday a particularly bad time to discover that your email infrastructure or sender reputation has a problem.

But most deliverability problems are preventable. You just need to work on them before your Black Friday campaign goes out, not after you see the results.

One of the biggest mistakes I see companies make around major shopping events is changing their sending behavior too abruptly. Let’s say your company normally sends 50,000 emails a week. Black Friday approaches, and suddenly you want to send 200,000 emails in a day.

To you, that looks like a holiday campaign. But to an inbox provider, it can look suspicious.

Email providers build a picture of your sending behavior over time. Sudden spikes can trigger throttling, which means an inbox provider slows down the rate at which it accepts your messages. So instead of delivering your campaign immediately, it may defer some emails and decide later whether to accept them.

That delay matters tremendously when your offer expires at midnight.

You want higher holiday volume to look like the natural progression of a healthy email program, not a completely different sender showing up overnight.

There’s another Black Friday tradition worth reconsidering: scheduling the big campaign for the same hour everyone else does. When thousands of brands send enormous campaigns at 8 or 9 a.m., inbox providers have to absorb a massive amount of traffic at once.

Your email service provider may tell you that your campaign has been “sent,” but that doesn’t mean every receiving server accepted every email immediately. Some providers may spread their delivery over a longer period. By the time an email reaches a customer, it could be competing with dozens of other promotions that arrived first.

There’s no prize for being part of the 9 a.m. stampede. There is value in reaching someone when their inbox isn’t experiencing its worst traffic jam of the year.

Your email list is another place where problems tend to hide until companies increase their volume.

Every invalid or poor-quality address you continue to contact creates unnecessary risk.

If your usual campaigns are relatively small, you may not notice the effect immediately. But when you increase your sending volume for Black Friday, those weaknesses become much more visible.

Before Cyber Week, validate your database and remove invalid addresses. Pay special attention to segments you haven’t contacted recently. This is also not the moment to resurrect a three-year-old list because someone on the team remembered you have it.

If thousands of people suddenly receive an email from a company they barely remember subscribing to, some are going to mark it as spam. Those complaints cause a lot of damage to your reputation – they’re direct feedback on how people feel about your emails.

Google recommends keeping spam complaint rates below 0.1% and avoiding 0.3% or higher. Yahoo also requires bulk senders to remain below a 0.3% complaint rate. With those thresholds, it doesn’t take thousands of angry customers to create a problem.

There are a few technical checks I’d consider non-negotiable before a major holiday campaign. Your domain should be properly authenticated with SPF, DKIM and DMARC.

Those acronyms may sound like something only your IT team should care about, but they answer a very basic question for an inbox provider: Is this email really coming from the company it claims to come from?

These are now part of the basic infrastructure of responsible commercial email.

If you don’t know whether your company has them configured properly, find out now. Not the Wednesday before Thanksgiving.

Founders often think about email performance after the send. What was our open rate? How many people clicked? What revenue did the campaign generate?

You’re smart to focus on these numbers, but sender reputation starts affecting your campaign before anyone has a chance to open it. Inbox providers consider your sending patterns, authentication, spam complaints, bounces and engagement when deciding where your emails belong.

A damaged reputation is difficult to repair in the middle of Cyber Week.

That’s why it’s helpful to monitor your sending domain and test your campaigns before the holiday rush. Check whether your domain or IP appears on blacklists. Test whether emails are reaching the inbox or spam folder. Review your bounce and complaint rates after every campaign leading up to Black Friday.

If something begins deteriorating, you want enough time to understand why.

There is very little you can do with that information on Friday morning when your biggest promotion of the year is already sitting in spam.

When companies have aggressive revenue targets, the temptation is to send to the largest possible audience. Consider doing the opposite: start with the people most likely to engage.

A smaller, healthier audience can often outperform a larger list that’s gone stale.

The biggest misconception about holiday email marketing is that success comes down to what happens on the day of the sale. In reality, much of the outcome has already been determined.

Your sender reputation has been developing for months. Your list has either been maintained or neglected. Your domain is either authenticated correctly or it isn’t. Your audience has either been hearing from you consistently or suddenly wondering who you are.

The companies in the best position on Black Friday are rarely the ones making frantic technical changes the night before. So before your team spends another hour debating a subject line:

You can spend weeks creating the perfect Black Friday offer. Make sure your customers actually get the chance to see it.

Black Friday is one of the few days of the year when customers expect companies to flood their inboxes. And flood them they do.

In 2025, brands using Mailchimp sent 1.39 billion emails on Black Friday alone. Cyber Monday brought another 1.3 billion. For founders preparing holiday campaigns, that volume creates a problem that has little to do with whether your subject line is clever or your discount is generous.

Your emails have to reach the inbox first.

#5300. The White House announced a raft of new tariffs on the same day inflation data came back at nearly twice the Fed’s target

The White House has announced a litany of new tariffs targeting imports from 14 economies, including key trading partners such as China and the EU. With consumers already stretched by an affordability crisis, the new duties come on the same day that the Bureau of Economic Analysis confirmed inflation hit 3.8%, according to the annual rate of the Personal Consumption Expenditures (PCE) price index, and nearly double the Federal Open Market Committee’s 2% goal.

The announcement has two important implications. First, though the new duties would be imposed on foreign economies, previous tariff studies indicate that 90% of the increased prices are ultimately borne by U.S. businesses and, more often than not, their consumers.

And second, it complicates the Federal Reserve’s next move. The Fed, now led by Kevin Warsh, raised rates in September for the first time since July 2023, to a range of 3.75% to 4%, and meets again Dec. 9–10.

Former Fed chairman Jerome Powell said that while tariffs represented a one-off price increase rather than broader inflationary factors, they nonetheless increased near-term inflation expectations. As UBS chief economist Paul Donovan told clients today: “The concern is the impact on U.S. inflation, and thus U.S. interest rates.”

And the Fed already has a data headache on its hands: The PCE increase to 3.8% compared with a year ago is nearly double the FOMC’s 2% target.

China faces a new 20% duty, and Vietnam, up to 35%, or 20% if it reaches a trade deal, according to Trade Representative Jamieson Greer, citing Section 301 of the Trade Act of 1974. Section 301 allows the U.S. to investigate foreign practices deemed unreasonable or discriminatory, or that burden or restrict U.S. commerce. Both nations are among the top 10 importers to the U.S., accounting for 7.8% and 7.4% of imports, respectively, per Census Bureau data.

Through September, the U.S. imported $215 billion in Chinese goods and $204.8 billion from Vietnam, which accounts for the largest U.S. trade deficit with any country, at $190.9 billion.

The European Union is also facing tariffs of 15%, while India is facing rates of up to 25%, or 17% in the event of a trade deal.

The new revenue-generating tariff action comes after the Supreme Court struck down Trump’s sweeping emergency tariffs in February, forcing the administration to refund roughly $100 billion of the $166 billion it had collected.

For most of the 14 economies, existing Section 301 duties count toward the new rate rather than being added on top. (China is the exception: Its 20% stacks on existing levies.) “In effect, it’ll look more like a top-up,” Greer told CNBC’s Squawk Box. “When it all nets out, it really will just top up a few percentage points.”

That will do little to calm the nerves of consumers who have been battling above-target inflation for more than five years. The New York Fed’s October survey of consumer expectations revealed that households expect inflation to be at 3.9% this time next year, and at 3.3% in three years’ time.

For the Fed, these heightened expectations can be a problem. Consumers may adjust their spending and saving, and make wage demands in response to their inflation expectations. That can create a self-reinforcing cycle, making inflation harder to bring down.

“The tariffs replace the previously announced Section 301 tariffs with a marginal incremental impact higher on goods prices but, moreover, set the table for further increases if negotiations break down,” Bradford Smith, portfolio manager at Janus Henderson Investors, told Fortune in a note.

“The announcement serves as a reminder that the Fed’s inflation fight is exacerbated by tariffs. With inflation already an issue and the Fed awaiting the lapping of previous tariff implementations, additional tariffs will make the Fed’s job more difficult.”

Eleanor Pringle is an award-winning senior reporter at Fortune covering news, the economy, and personal finance. Eleanor previously worked as a business correspondent and news editor in regional news in the U.K. She completed her journalism training with the Press Association after earning a degree from the University of East Anglia.

#5299. Beyond Nvidia: Convoy co-founder and former Microsoft leader raise $277M to rethink AI infrastructure

by Todd Bishop on Nov 23, 2026 at 4:30 amNovember 23, 2026 at 1:27 pm

Former Microsoft executives Dan Lewis and Kutta Srinivasan have raised $277 million on a bet that the next wave of AI will run on a very different kind of data center.

The outsized seed funding for their new startup, Marlowe, reflects the scale of the challenge they’re taking on. As AI shifts from training models to running them in everyday products, Marlowe designs and operates computing systems for that work. It’s starting with chips from AMD and Etched, expanding beyond the Nvidia GPUs that have fueled the AI boom.

They say tuning the chips, networking and software for specific AI workloads and applications will maximize performance and efficiency, lowering costs as a result.

The new funding values Marlowe at $1.15 billion, according to the company, making it a unicorn out of the gate. Accel led the latest round, joined by a long list of big names in tech and finance, from KKR co-founder Henry Kravis to Uber CEO Dara Khosrowshahi.

Lewis, Marlowe’s CEO, previously co-founded the trucking startup Convoy and later was an enterprise AI leader at Microsoft, where Srinivasan, now Marlowe’s CTO, was a corporate vice president and the company-wide technical lead for AI infrastructure.

“The demand for intelligence and AI is very high,” Lewis said in an interview, when asked how a former freight marketplace CEO ended up in AI computing. “It’s something that should be accessible and affordable for everyone.”

Marlowe, founded in May, is based in both Bellevue, Wash., and Redwood City, Calif., and is approaching 30 employees. Lewis said the two home bases reflect where its customers, partners and talent are concentrated, pointing to Bellevue as an emerging AI hub.

Lewis, a former Amazon general manager, joined Flexport as a technical advisor when the freight company acquired Convoy’s technology after the startup’s abrupt shutdown in 2023. In February 2025, he returned to Microsoft, where he had also worked previously, as a chief product officer focused on enterprise AI, later becoming a corporate vice president.

GeekWire first reported in June that he had left Microsoft to launch a new startup, but he wasn’t ready to share details at the time.

From Microsoft to Marlowe: The founders said the idea for Marlowe grew out of what they saw at Microsoft: demand was surging for inference, running AI models in products and services, but data centers were still being built mainly for training those models in the first place.

“We were always oversold, effectively sold out,” Lewis said.

Since then, demand for inference has grown faster than supply, pushing up costs at the same time that power shortages, permitting and financing are making new data centers harder to build. The company cites a 40% increase in data center construction costs since 2020, which makes every watt more valuable.

The company isn’t using Nvidia chips for now, but it hasn’t ruled them out.

Its first site, built around Etched’s chips, is scheduled to go live in December, the founders said. A second, larger site using AMD’s new Helios systems is on track for the second quarter of 2027.

Both sites are under contract, and a third is under a letter of intent. The company says it has signed three customer agreements but isn’t yet naming the customers or the locations.

Srinivasan said that at the big tech companies where he has worked, chips from vendors other than Nvidia made up a small slice of the fleet. When a new AI model came out, the top engineers focused on getting it running on the Nvidia chips, and the rest got left behind.

“There were literally times when a significant portion of our non-Nvidia fleet was either idle or grossly underused or didn’t support the latest models and workloads,” he said.

That’s the gap Marlowe is trying to close. Its engineers work directly on customers’ workloads to get other chips performing at their full potential, giving those companies a way to reduce their dependence on a single supplier.

Marlowe says gains of 10% to 20% at each layer of the system, from chips and networking to power management and software, add up to two to three times more output per watt and per dollar than conventional GPU clouds, measured in tokens, the chunks of text that AI models process and generate.

Competition and funding: Marlowe isn’t alone in the bet. Gimlet Labs, which raised $300 million at a $3 billion valuation in September, and General Compute, which raised $100 million in October, are also building inference clouds that run on a mix of chips.

CoreWeave, the largest of the so-called neoclouds, rents out computing power built almost entirely on Nvidia chips. Nvidia held about 47 million CoreWeave shares as of Sept. 30, and CoreWeave has taken on about $47 billion in debt to build out its data centers.

Marlowe’s launch also comes during a turbulent stretch for Nvidia. The company’s board reinstated Jensen Huang as CEO on Monday, less than two weeks after his resignation.

Much of Marlowe’s funding will go toward chips, networking equipment and the support needed to run the sites, along with hiring, the founders said. By the standards of AI infrastructure, $277 million doesn’t go far.

Rather than chasing giant facilities, Marlowe plans to prove its approach at sites of tens of megawatts and then finance more capacity site by site, Lewis said. He noted that some startups have raised four to five times as much and will deploy a little less computing power on a similar timeline.

The $277 million includes a smaller initial round led by Eclipse, Lewis said. Eclipse founder and CEO Lior Susan is Marlowe’s executive chairman, and Ido Susan, founder and CEO of the data center networking company DriveNets, is on the board. Other backers include Bessemer, Altimeter, Atreides, Journey and Valor.

Angel investors also include Box CEO Aaron Levie and former LinkedIn CEO Ryan Roslansky. Mark Okerstrom, the former Expedia CFO and CEO who later served as Convoy’s president, is also an investor.

Past lives: Srinivasan’s career runs from video games to AI infrastructure. In an earlier stint at Microsoft, he worked on DirectX and games including Halo 3, then spent eight years at Valve, where he led the team that built the first Steam mobile app.

He later served as the lead architect for machine learning training infrastructure at Facebook, and as a technical fellow at LinkedIn before moving to Microsoft’s CoreAI group in 2025.

Marlowe is a very different business from Convoy, the digital freight marketplace Lewis co-founded to match truckers with shippers. Convoy reached a $3.8 billion valuation before shutting down in 2023, amid a freight recession and a pullback in venture funding.

Asked how Marlowe would avoid getting similarly squeezed by forces outside its control in a capital-intensive business, Lewis said the industry is at “the very beginning” of a long-term shift in how people use AI and data.

He also pointed to a mix of long- and short-term contracts and multiple customers, rather than one big customer that could pull out.

Ultimately, Lewis said he believes Marlowe’s edge will come down to having the engineering skills to get the most out of new chips. “You can’t just take a new chip that comes out and plug it in and expect it to produce tokens,” he said. “You have to go do the work.”

Updated at 6:20 a.m. PT with Nvidia’s reinstatement of Jensen Huang as CEO.
